I trained a small PII detector for PrivAiTe, my local proxy that masks personal data before a prompt reaches an LLM: crp4222/privaite-pii-minilm.
It is a multilingual MiniLM (117M parameters, 15 types from names and contacts to IDs, bank details and secrets), trained only on datasets whose licenses allow commercial use, released under BSD 3-Clause, with PyTorch, ONNX fp32 and int8, and Core ML builds.
On 9 public test sets it never saw, it masks as many person names as the best of GLiNER PII, NVIDIA GLiNER-PII, GLiNER2, Piiranha and OpenAI privacy-filter, or more, on 6 of them, usually with higher precision. It trails GLiNER PII on short lowercase voice requests and NVIDIA on court rulings.
It is also 2.5 to 7 times smaller and much faster: 9 ms per 1,000 characters on an M1 Pro Neural Engine and 23 ms on CPU in int8, against 186 to 621 ms for the others on the same machine and documents. Numbers, test sets and limits are on the card:
crp4222/privaite-pii-minilm

Hi everyone! I want to share a few updates about GRM development.
*GRM-3.4 has been canceled*
Although GRM-3.4 showed strong reasoning and coding capabilities, testing revealed several issues. It tended to overthink, and its code often contained errors that GRM-3.2-Sky handled correctly. Its tool use also needed improvement, and its terminal performance did not reach the level we were aiming for.
We repeatedly saw it rewrite files from scratch instead of using editing tools, and use shell commands to create or modify files when dedicated tools were available.
*Looking ahead to GRM-3.6*
GRM-3.6 is a possible next generation for the GRM models. We are still deciding whether it will be a single large model or a complete model family. The flagship is set to be **GRM-3.6-Moon**, a **35B-A3B** model.
*Experimental models*
Orion LLM Labs may release experimental models more regularly from now on. These experiments will help us research and test ideas for future GRM models.
Thanks for following the project!

Can a network whose trunk is only XOR, table lookups and integer adds learn Connect Four?
Partly. I trained a GF(2⁸) integer model (8.4M params, CPU-only) on 320k games labelled by a negamax search teacher.
What it learned:
• agrees with the teacher on 59.6% of training / 41.0% of board-disjoint holdout positions
• beats a random player 85.2% of the time
What it didn't:
• loses to a 1-ply "win now / block now" rule (wins 37.2%)
• loses to 2-ply lookahead (wins 24.3%)
Agreeing with a teacher is not the same as playing well, and this release measures both.
Caveat up front: the float32 read-out is 99.6% of the parameters. The trunk is float-free; the full model isn't yet.

One Qwen3-VL-8B checkpoint improves all three streaming spatial benchmarks at once: OST-Bench 50.52 to 63.93 (+13.41), UCS-Bench +7.44, OVO-S-Bench +4.91. The change is in the supervision, with no new memory module or annotation.
The ChronoReplay paper calls the failure mode interface lock-in: post-train on one answer format and that readout improves while others stall. A categorical-only control hits 58.03 on OVO-S but drops OST from 50.52 to 47.48.
🔍 The recipe
• Keep targets in native formats (option, metric value with units, timestamp)
• Replay episodes in source order, each target attached to its causal prefix
• Loss mass: 2/3 on 33,180 single-turn examples, 1/3 on 6,381 episodes (alpha = 0.5)
📊 The numbers
• Three-benchmark mean 56.86, against 50.74 (categorical-only) and 50.76 (trajectory-only)
• Chronological order beats a shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points on two seeds; the 13.41 belongs to the whole recipe
• Adaptive frame selection adds +4.09 on OVO-S (57.98) with 80.50 frames instead of 128
⚠️ Caveats
• One backbone, indoor scenes only; the single-family comparison is confounded by data coverage
• The repo has a CPU smoke test and a --dry-run training command, but no license and no fine-tuned weights

Hi everyone! I want to share a few updates about GRM development.

Although GRM-3.4 showed strong reasoning and coding capabilities, testing revealed several issues. It tended to overthink, and its code often contained errors that GRM-3.2-Sky handled correctly. Its tool use also needed improvement, and its terminal performance did not reach the level we were aiming for.
We repeatedly saw it rewrite files from scratch instead of using editing tools, and use shell commands to create or modify files when dedicated tools were available.

GRM-3.6 is a possible next generation for the GRM models. We are still deciding whether it will be a single large model or a complete model family. The flagship is set to be **GRM-3.6-Moon**, a **35B-A3B** model.
Orion LLM Labs may release experimental models more regularly from now on. These experiments will help us research and test ideas for future GRM models.

1. Introduction
In Nanbeige4.3, we take a foundational step toward pushing the boundaries of lightweight agents. Our strategy centers on building a high-capacity teacher agent first, which will subsequently anchor the distillation of advanced agentic capabilities into smaller models.
To this end, we first introduce Nanbeige4.3-33B, designed as the flagship teacher model for the Nanbeige4.3 series. Delivering state-of-the-art agentic performance among open models in the ~30B parameter class, Nanbeige4.3-33B excels at complex coding and professional cowork tasks. It not only offers a powerful, cost-effective option for immediate real-world deployment, but also lays the necessary foundation to power our upcoming small model distillation pipeline (e.g., for Nanbeige4.3-3B).
2. Model Performance
We compare Nanbeige4.3-33B with recently released frontier models at around the 30B-parameter scale: Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B, and Gemma4-31B. All models are evaluated at their highest thinking effort. For each benchmark, we use the same inference hyperparameters and harness across models.

3. Quickstart
The tokenizer provides a configurable chat template for reasoning and tool-use scenarios:
enable_thinking
controls whether the model generates reasoning for the current response. It is enabled by default; set it to
False
for non-thinking mode.
preserve_thinking
controls whether reasoning from previous assistant turns is retained in a multi-turn conversation. We recommend
False
for general chat and question answering, and
True
for multi-turn tool use, office tasks, and code-agent workflows.
Passing
tools
enables the tool-use template. We recommend
tool_call_format="xml"
for the best tool-calling performance;
json
is also supported for compatibility.
The model supports a context length of up to 524,288 tokens (512K).

Prompt Encoding
This release does not include a Jinja-format chat template. The
encoding
folder contains a self-contained Python reference implementation (
encoding.py
) with test cases for multi-turn conversations, tool calling, thinking mode, numeric reasoning effort, mid-conversation system messages, and interleaved image content.
For production use, we additionally release
deepseek-recipe
, a set of Rust libraries with Python bindings that provides the same prompt format as a maintained, protocol-aware toolkit. It converts Messages, Chat Completions, and Responses API requests into the Conversation format, encodes them into DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 prompts or token IDs, and parses model output back into complete or streamed responses — covering thinking, tool calls, images, and generation settings. Model inference, tool execution, and HTTP transport are left to the caller.

LFM3-1.7B
LFM3-1.7B is a
text model for local agents and specialized applications
, based on our new tri-hybrid architecture.
Agentic training:
post-trained for agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw, with a 256K-token context window.
Designed for the edge:
at 4-bit precision, it takes about 1 GB of memory, so it fits on any phone or laptop.
Made to be specialized:
adapt the model to your domains, formats, and tools via quick single-GPU fine-tuning.
Find more information about the LFM3 family in
our release blog post
.

Chat template
LFM3 uses this ChatML format, generated from the checkpoint's
chat template
:
<|startoftext|><|im_start|>system
You are a helpful assistant trained by Liquid AI.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Explain how a heat pump works.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>
Use
tokenizer.apply_chat_template()
with
add_generation_prompt=True
to format messages automatically.
Reasoning is enabled by default. You can set
enable_thinking=False
to disable thinking traces, but this behavior can be inconsistent, especially for reasoning-heavy tasks.
Reasoning from turns before the latest user message is removed unless
preserve_thinking=True
.
Tool calling
Pass function schemas through
tools=...
to
apply_chat_template()
. The template formats tool definitions and results automatically. Generated calls use XML:
<tool_call>
<function=get_weather>
<parameter=city>
Paris
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
Execute the call in your application. Add the parsed assistant call to history as a
tool_calls
entry, then append the result as a
tool
message. Keep passing the tool schemas on subsequent requests and preserve the assistant's content and reasoning from the current tool-use turn.
function.arguments
must be a Python mapping. Decode JSON strings with
json.loads()
before applying the template.
Tool search
LFM3 supports deferred tools. Set
defer_loading=True
to keep tool definitions out of the prompt until your harness's search tool returns their names as
tool_reference
parts. The chat template then inserts their definitions into
<additional_tools>
.
tools = [
search_tool,
{
"type"
:
"function"
,
"defer_loading"
:
True
,
"function"
: get_weather_schema},
]
messages.append({
"role"
:
"tool"
,

: call_id,

: [
{

},

Edge inference
At 32K context, LFM3-1.7B prefills at least 2.5x faster and decodes at least 1.8x faster than every compared model on all three devices, while using the least memory.
Evaluation details
All models run as Q4_0 GGUF files in llama.cpp with 32,768 tokens of context, batch size 1, 100 output tokens, and GPU offload. Prefill is the prompt processing speed and decode is the generation speed, both in tokens per second. LFM3-1.7B uses a llama.cpp build with LFM3 support, and the other models use llama.cpp release b11744.
AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395

GPU inference
At 1,024 concurrent requests, LFM3-1.7B can produce 3.6 billion tokens/day on one NVIDIA B300.
Training
Pre-training:
two stages build LFM3-1.7B-Base on 22T tokens in total.
Main pre-training:
compared with LFM2, the mix adds more scientific papers, repository-level code, math, and a wider range of knowledge sources.
Mid-training:
the last 3.5T tokens use curated, higher-quality data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls. This stage also extends the context window to 256K tokens.
Post-training:
four stages develop conversation, reasoning, and tool-use capabilities.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT):
1.75T tokens across various tasks, including chat, reasoning, tool calling, and agentic traces.
Mixed reinforcement learning:
many domains trained at once, from math and code to SQL and structured outputs. A length penalty in the reward keeps answers concise.
Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD):
six specialist RL teachers (code, math, tool use, long context, agentic work, and enterprise workflows) are distilled back into a single model.
Agentic RL:
tasks from web browsing to office work are run inside real agent harnesses, preparing the model for deployment.

Model Overview
Description
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe is an offline speech and audio model that processes recordings, together with text instructions and optional context, into text responses.
NVIDIA developed this
Speech-Augmented Language Model (SALM)
for multilingual transcription, speech translation, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, timestamp prediction, language identification, and audio question answering. The training mixture also includes a small amount of text instruction following and PII tagging/redaction tasks.
This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use.

Efficiency
With the optimized vLLM implementation in the Nemotron Transcribe NIM, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU transcribes up to 2,238 seconds of audio per second (NVFP4 with DFlash2 speculative decoding) and returns the transcript of a 30-second recording in 0.13 seconds. These serving optimizations are not yet part of the open-source release; we aim to upstream them to NeMo Speech and vLLM at a later date. The vLLM integration shipped in NeMo Speech on the release day is intended for model development and is expected to be roughly two times slower.

Model Architecture
Architecture Type:
Other - hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model with a Transformer audio encoder
Network Architecture:
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE with Transformer ASR encoder and Sortformer speaker encoder
Design:
Audio perception module consisting of transformer ASR encoder and
Nemotron-3-Diarization
speaker encoder, a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) timestamp alignment head, and
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B
language backbone. The perception configuration uses a 1,280-dimensional identity connector followed by a learned projection to 2,688 dimensions. Audio features are combined with the text prompt for text generation. The model enables joint multi-token prediction (MTP), with two trained next-token prediction depths using a repeated layer and retaining the existing head. Reusing the repeated layer during inference supports up to eight speculative tokens. A dedicated
DFlash2
draft model, a block-diffusion drafter based on DFlash, is also provided as an option for speculative decoding.
Base model:
nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16
; 600M parameter pretrained ASR transformer; and approximately 99M parameter Nemotron-3-Diarization speaker encoder.
Parameter count:
The language backbone has approximately 3.5B active parameters. Together with the approximately 800M-parameter joint audio encoder, the model has approximately 4.3B active parameters.
Precision:
Weights are released in bfloat16 (BF16), with FP8 and NVFP4 quantized variants.

Inputs
Property
Draft specification
Types
Audio and text.
Formats
Audio: .wav, .flac, .mp3, .ogg (any format that can be decoded to PCM). Text: String (plain text or chat messages).
Parameters
Audio: one-dimensional waveform per processed channel. Text: one-dimensional token sequence.
Sampling and preprocessing
Recipe audio sampling rate: 16 kHz. Use the exported model's preprocessor and
nemotron3p5
prompt format. Encoder feature stride is configured as approximately 80 ms per audio token equivalent.
Limits
The model is trained with recordings up to 1 hour long, and its maximum context size in training was 65536 tokens. It is not guaranteed to generalize beyond these limits.
Audio chunking
The encoder uses 30-second post-feature chunks. This is an internal processing choice, not a 30-second recording limit or a streaming latency claim.
Language coverage

40-language support matrix

Other Properties Related to Input:
The model processes 16kHz single-channel audio decoded to a float32 PCM waveform. The maximum supported audio length is up to 1 hour.

Training Dataset
Data Modality:
Audio, Text
Audio Training Data Size:
More than 1 Million Hours (approximately 1.72 million hours across unique indexed audio examples; 6.53 million hours including repeated exposure)
Text Training Data Size:
1 Billion to 10 Trillion Tokens (5.6 billion unique tokens)
Data Collection Method by dataset:
Hybrid: Manually-Collected, Automated, Synthetic
Labeling Method by dataset:
Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automatic/Sensors, Synthetic
Properties:
Approximately 372 million unique audio examples (1.72 million hours) and 5.6 billion unique text tokens. Audio is paired with text instructions and targets: transcripts, translations, speaker-attributed transcripts, captions, answers, and labels; a small share of the data is text-only. The content comprises public and third-party speech corpora (read speech, conversations, meetings, broadcasts, and earnings calls), web-derived speech, sound, and music, pseudo-labeled transcripts and translations, constructed multi-speaker mixtures, and synthetic data such as synthetic PII text and speech. The data covers the 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, as well as code-switched speech.
Training Data Size Details
Total examples, audio hours, text tokens, unique dataset count, partition percentages, and collection periods:
Total multimodal tokens (non-unique): 479 billion
Audio share of multimodal input positions: approx. 60%

Processing:
Source manifests provide audio references, labels, conversations, and task metadata. The mixture includes human-labeled and pseudo-labeled transcriptions and translations with corresponding instruction prompts. Task-preference sampling selects among transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, text normalization, captioning, and code-switched targets.
Harmful-content processing:
The training mixture includes text and audio safety-tuning subsets and selected filtered or human-curated components.
Public Summary of Training Content:
Granary v2 multilingual speech data:
multilingual data covering ASR, speech translation, contextual and code-switched ASR, speech QA, ITN, captioning, long-form transcription, language identification, PII-aware ASR, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants.
Multi-speaker ASR data:
meeting, conversational, and synthetic multi-speaker mixtures, including source material from AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI, ICSI, DiPCo, Fisher/FisherHQ, and Multilingual LibriSpeech.
Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotation data:
used for paralinguistic event and style-token prediction.
Audio understanding data:
sound, music, and speech understanding; audio reasoning; spoken instruction following; and safety tuning. Its source families include AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, CREMA-D, and related audio-instruction mixtures.
Text-only instruction-tuning data:
instruction following, reasoning, coding, tool use, multilingual, and safety subsets.
PII-focused data:
Nemotron-PII text SFT plus synthetic PII-aware ASR
No-speech abstention data:
derived from AudioSet and non-speech audio understanding training data
Transcribe's training data includes data licensed from David AI. The DAI-ASR-I18N evaluation set was not part of it.
Public Datasets
The Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe training recipe uses public source datasets both directly and through NVIDIA-created derivatives, including AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI Meeting Corpus, DiPCo, Europarl, Google Speech Commands, ICSI Meeting Corpus, Libri-Light, LibriSpeech, MOSEL, Multilingual LibriSpeech, National Speech Corpus 1 and 6, ReazonSpeech v2, The People's Speech 12k, VCTK, VoxPopuli, and YTC.
Additional externally available source families used by the recipe include
Granary v2
, Common Voice 26, YODAS2, FLEURS, DUSHA, Golos, M-AILABS, Falar, SOVA, AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, and CREMA-D.
Nemotron-PII
is an NVIDIA-produced synthetic dataset with a public dataset card.
Private Datasets
The training mixture includes the following third-party, vendor-provided, or internally curated source families:
Third-party speech corpora:
Fisher/FisherHQ, Switchboard, Wall Street Journal, and SPGISpeech
Vendor-provided multilingual and multi-speaker data:
DavidAI D12a/D12b/D12c and MLC-SLM-2
Internal derivative datasets:
multi-speaker task variants, non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations, PII-aware ASR data, language-identification data, and no-speech abstention data
Data Crawling and Scraping
Some upstream source families are web-derived. These include YODAS/YODAS2 and YTC, as well as publicly available internet scale data represented in AudioSet and related audio-understanding and no-speech datasets. The audio understanding mixture and the pretrained base components may also contain web-derived data.
Internally Generated Data, Including Prompt-Collected Data
NVIDIA-generated or NVIDIA-transformed training artifacts include:
Granary v2 pseudo-transcriptions and model-generated translations, together with human-improved and Riva-labeled variants
Prompt-controlled Granary v2 task expansions for transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, inverse text normalization, disfluency-reduced transcription, captioning, and code-switched transcription
Fine-, coarse-, distractor-, partial-, and negative-context variants for contextual ASR
Long-form transcription data and transcript-plus-QA, timestamp, speaker-tag, and translation variants
Multi-speaker task formatting and constructed audio mixtures
Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations
Balanced language-identification prompts and targets
PII tagging and redaction examples
No-speech abstention prompts and empty-response targets
Curated Nemotron text SFT data, audio-instruction, audio-reasoning, and safety-tuning blends
Training prompts are developer-authored or generated task instructions associated with prepared training examples. User interactions with a deployed product or model were not used to train the model.
Self-Sourced Synthetic Data
Synthetic and model-generated training data include:
Nemotron-PII text data:
fully synthetic text examples covering more than 55 PII/PHI categories, with tagged and redacted outputs
PII-aware ASR data:
synthetic multilingual PII-positive speech examples
Constructed multi-speaker mixtures:
AuMix examples combining source recordings into conversations of up to eight speakers, including long-form mixtures
Granary v2 task variants:
generated contextual terms and distractors, speech questions and answers, captions, code-switched targets, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants
Audio understanding synthetic-data-generation subsets:
generated captions, questions, answers, instruction-following targets, and reasoning traces for sound, music, speech, and audio-reasoning tasks
Prompt augmentation:
deterministic and generated prompt variants for transcription, language identification, PII handling, and no-speech abstention
Pseudo-labeled ASR and translation examples retain source audio and use model-generated labels; they should not be described as synthetic audio. Constructed multi-speaker mixtures likewise combine source recordings rather than generating new speaker identities.

Data count:
more than 330,000 test examples from public benchmarks, including approximately 243,000 for English, multilingual, multi-speaker, and contextual transcription; 29,000 for language identification; and 57,000 for audio understanding, voice instruction following, and text-only reasoning. Speech translation, long-form, code-switched, and entity benchmarks are evaluated in addition.
Modalities:
audio with text instructions, references, and context; text-only for the text reasoning benchmarks.
Nature of the content:
read speech (LibriSpeech, Multilingual LibriSpeech, FLEURS, Common Voice), parliamentary speech (VoxPopuli), podcasts and online video (GigaSpeech), financial earnings calls (Earnings-22, SPGISpeech), meetings (AMI, NOTSOFAR-1, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting), telephone conversations (CALLHOME), interviews (Mixer 6), noisy and degraded recordings (URGENT 2024), code-switched conversations, spoken questions and instructions (VoiceBench, Spoken-MQA), and speech, sound, and music for audio understanding (MMAU, MMAR, AIR-Bench).
Linguistic characteristics:
40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, including Indian-accented English and Hindi (Monsoon), Mandarin meetings, and Hindi–English, Bengali–English, and Mandarin–English code-switching; transcripts are scored both verbatim and in normalized written form, depending on the benchmark.

Start the Server
Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8):
export
VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm
# Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds).
export
VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600
export
VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180
# Word timestamps require the V1 model runner.
export
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0
vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \
--served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \
--trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \
--max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \
--enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \
--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \
--mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \
--limit-mm-per-prompt
'{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}'
\
--speculative-config
'{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}'
\
--reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \
--trust-request-mm-kwargs \
--middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware
The server listens on
127.0.0.1:8000
; use
--host
and
--port

--gpu-memory-utilization
,
--max-model-len

--max-num-seqs
. The
--middleware
and

Speculative Decoding
Speculative decoding proposes several tokens at once and verifies them with the main model. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers.
The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. Approximate throughput for batched English ASR on
one NVIDIA H100 80 GB
, using tuned serving settings:
Decoding mode
Approximate BF16 RTFx
MTP off
Not measured
MTP2
410
MTP8
270
DFlash2 K=7
340
DFlash2 K=15
260
RTFx is total audio duration divided by processing time: 340 RTFx means about 340 seconds of audio processed per second under batch load. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate.
Keep ReplaySSM (
--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none
) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model
As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model
nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2
proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's
dflash
method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload.
vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment:
python - <<
'EOF_PATCH'
from pathlib import Path
import vllm
path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent /
"model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py"
source
= path.read_text()
if
"safe_anchor_token_ids"
not
in
source
:
old =
"    successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n"
anchor =
"            anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),"
assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1,
"unexpected vLLM version"
source
= source.replace(old, (
"    safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n"
"        min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n"
"    )\n"
+ old
)).replace(anchor,
"            safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),"
)
path.write_text(
source
)
EOF_PATCH

Generation-Loop Guardrail
In rare cases, the model can fail to terminate generation and fall into a loop. In these cases, we recommend applying the following function once to the final decoded output, before scoring or returning it:
import
re
CHAR_RUN = re.
compile
(
r"(.)\1{20,}"
, re.DOTALL)
BLOCK_RUN = re.
compile
(
r"(.{1,4096}?)\1{19,}"
, re.DOTALL)
def
cleanup_generation_loops
(
text:
str
) ->
str
:
# Collapse a character repeated ≥21 times to one copy.
text = CHAR_RUN.sub(
lambda
m: m.group(
1
), text)
# Collapse an exact 1–4096-character block repeated ≥20 times.
return
BLOCK_RUN.sub(
lambda
m: m.group(
1
), text)

Intended Task/Domain:
Speech transcription and translation, contextual and speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, language identification, and audio/text question answering.
Model Type:
Speech/audio encoder with speaker-aware perception, projection to a mixture-of-experts autoregressive language model, and joint MTP.
Intended Users:
Developers and researchers building speech and audio applications with application-specific evaluation and review.
Output:
Generated text, optionally containing task-specific speaker/event tags or PII annotations. When timestamp capture is enabled in vLLM, the response also includes
word timestamps, diarization segments, and a mapping between transcript speaker tags and diarization speakers
. Conversation history must be supplied by the application; persistent memory is not established by this recipe.
Tools evaluating synthetic data and authenticity
The pipeline includes transcript classification, annotation/span checks, multiple-model-agreement based high quality filtering metrics, and judge based filtering for preference transcription instruction answers.
Describe how the model works:
The model preprocesses 16-kHz audio and encodes it into features. The configured speaker-aware encoder contributes speaker information. Features pass through the perception projection and are combined with the text prompt. The language backbone predicts output text autoregressively. When requested, the bundled CTC heads align the generated transcript to the audio, and the speaker encoder supplies diarization segments. Two trained MTP depths supply auxiliary training objectives, and the repeated layer can be reused for speculative decoding.

Technical Limitations & Mitigation:
Errors include substitutions, deletions, repetitions, hallucinated speech, incorrect language choice, and speaker attribution errors. Targeted testing is recommended for long recordings, overlapping speakers, noise, names, code-switching, and misleading context. Performance on text-only tasks, without audio input, is not as good as on audio tasks: text-only reasoning and instruction following were not a primary training objective, and the model scores below its base language model on text-only benchmarks. Audio understanding, reasoning, and spoken instruction following were evaluated only in English and may not work reliably in other languages.
Verified to meet prescribed NVIDIA quality standards:
Yes.
Performance Metrics:
The evaluation plan covers WER/CER and corpus-specific variants; context-biasing WER, named-entity WER, named-entity false-negative rate, and entity F1; multi-speaker cpWER/tcpWER; translation BLEU/spBLEU/COMET; language-identification accuracy; word-level timestamp accuracy; instruction-following scores; benchmark-specific hallucination and event metrics; and serving latency/throughput.
Potential Known Risks:
The model may misrepresent a recording and generate a plausible transcript or answer. Speaker tags may not always attribute statements to the correct person.
When context is supplied, it can influence the output toward incorrect or irrelevant terms, and the model's robustness to misleading context has not been fully established across all supported settings. Any explanations the model generates should not be taken as verified causal accounts of the model's prediction.
The model was optimized explicitly for instruction following and as such is more susceptible to prompt injection and jailbreaking in various forms as a result of its instruction tuning. This means that the model should be paired with additional rails or system filtering to limit exposure to instructions from malicious sources -- either directly or indirectly by retrieval (e.g. via visiting a website) -- as they may yield outputs that can lead to harmful, system-level outcomes up to and including remote code execution in agentic systems when effective security controls including guardrails are not in place. The model may generate answers that may be inaccurate, omit key information, include irrelevant or redundant text, or produce socially unacceptable or undesirable text, even if the prompt itself does not include anything explicitly offensive.

Audio perception module consisting of transformer ASR encoder and
speaker encoder, a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) timestamp alignment head, and

language backbone. The perception configuration uses a 1,280-dimensional identity connector followed by a learned projection to 2,688 dimensions. Audio features are combined with the text prompt for text generation. The model enables joint multi-token prediction (MTP), with two trained next-token prediction depths using a repeated layer and retaining the existing head. Reusing the repeated layer during inference supports up to eight speculative tokens. A dedicated
draft model, a block-diffusion drafter based on DFlash, is also provided as an option for speculative decoding.

Tools evaluating synthetic data and authenticity

The pipeline includes transcript classification, annotation/span checks, multiple-model-agreement based high quality filtering metrics, and judge based filtering for preference transcription instruction answers.

The model preprocesses 16-kHz audio and encodes it into features. The configured speaker-aware encoder contributes speaker information. Features pass through the perception projection and are combined with the text prompt. The language backbone predicts output text autoregressively. When requested, the bundled CTC heads align the generated transcript to the audio, and the speaker encoder supplies diarization segments. Two trained MTP depths supply auxiliary training objectives, and the repeated layer can be reused for speculative decoding.
List the groups (or group characteristics) for which this was tested to produce comparable outcomes:

Errors include substitutions, deletions, repetitions, hallucinated speech, incorrect language choice, and speaker attribution errors. Targeted testing is recommended for long recordings, overlapping speakers, noise, names, code-switching, and misleading context. Performance on text-only tasks, without audio input, is not as good as on audio tasks: text-only reasoning and instruction following were not a primary training objective, and the model scores below its base language model on text-only benchmarks. Audio understanding, reasoning, and spoken instruction following were evaluated only in English and may not work reliably in other languages.
Verified to meet prescribed NVIDIA quality standards:

The evaluation plan covers WER/CER and corpus-specific variants; context-biasing WER, named-entity WER, named-entity false-negative rate, and entity F1; multi-speaker cpWER/tcpWER; translation BLEU/spBLEU/COMET; language-identification accuracy; word-level timestamp accuracy; instruction-following scores; benchmark-specific hallucination and event metrics; and serving latency/throughput.
The model may misrepresent a recording and generate a plausible transcript or answer. Speaker tags may not always attribute statements to the correct person.

When context is supplied, it can influence the output toward incorrect or irrelevant terms, and the model's robustness to misleading context has not been fully established across all supported settings. Any explanations the model generates should not be taken as verified causal accounts of the model's prediction.

The model was optimized explicitly for instruction following and as such is more susceptible to prompt injection and jailbreaking in various forms as a result of its instruction tuning. This means that the model should be paired with additional rails or system filtering to limit exposure to instructions from malicious sources -- either directly or indirectly by retrieval (e.g. via visiting a website) -- as they may yield outputs that can lead to harmful, system-level outcomes up to and including remote code execution in agentic systems when effective security controls including guardrails are not in place. The model may generate answers that may be inaccurate, omit key information, include irrelevant or redundant text, or produce socially unacceptable or undesirable text, even if the prompt itself does not include anything explicitly offensive.

Mistral Large 4 - Le Chonk
Mistral Large 4 is our largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe.
Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union.
Find more information on our
blog
. The model is also served on the
Mistral API
as
mistral-large-4
.
The checkpoint ships with an embedded DSpark speculative decoding draft head — see
Speculative decoding (DSpark)
.
A quantized
NVFP4 checkpoint
is also available, with a smaller memory footprint, faster inference and same performance. It targets Blackwell GPUs and supports vLLM and SGLang.
Key Features
Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices:
~1T total / ~52B active parameters
: granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert.
1M context length
, for long-context workloads.
Multimodal input
: accepts text and image input, with text output. Pixtral-style vision encoder trained to handle variable image sizes and aspect ratios.
Instruct and Reasoning functionalities
with function calls, reasoning effort configurable per request.
Mistral Large 4 offers the following capabilities:
Reasoning Mode
: three reasoning efforts —
low
,
medium
,
high
(default) — so the same model can answer a quick chat reply or work through a complex agentic run.
Vision
: analyzes images, charts, technical drawings, and documents, with state-of-the-art visual grounding among open weights.
Multilingual
: natively fluent in 160+ languages, including all official languages of the European Union.
System Prompt
: strong adherence and support for system prompts.
Agentic
: native function calling, JSON output, and strict JSON schema enforcement.
Cybersecurity
: state of the art among open-weight models for security work, while refusing malicious requests.
Large Context Window
: supports a 1M context window.
We release this model under the
Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License
: a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral.
Recommended Settings
Reasoning Effort
:
'low'
/
'medium'
/
'high'
— default is
'high'
.
Use
reasoning_effort="high"
for complex prompts and agentic usage,
'low'
for fast chat replies and
'medium'
for day to day usage.
Sampling
: for all reasoning efforts, we recommend the following sampling parameters:
temperature=1.0
top_p=0.95
System Prompt
: define a clear environment and use case, including guidance on how to effectively leverage tools in agentic systems.
Tools
: keep the set of tools well-defined and limit their number to the minimum required for the use case.
Context
: the checkpoint supports a 1M context window.
Benchmarks
We compared Mistral Large 4 with recent open-weight models. We report results on agentic coding and global intelligence here; for more benchmarks, especially on cybersecurity, finance and law, see our
blog post
.
Agentic Coding
Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.
On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, ML4 scores
48%
, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using
47%
fewer tokens per task on average.
Global Intelligence
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, Mistral Large 4 scores
26
, the highest among western open-weight models. The leading open-weight models from China score higher on this aggregate index, but Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong on coding and cybersecurity, as shown in our
blog post
.

vLLM (Recommended)
We recommend using Mistral Large 4 with the
vLLM library
for production-ready inference.
See also the
vLLM recipe for Mistral Large 4
for ready-made serving configurations.
Installation
Use the official vLLM Docker image, which includes support for Mistral Large 4:
docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4
Serve the Model
We recommend a server/client setup:
docker run --runtime nvidia --gpus all \
-v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
-p 8000:8000 \
--ipc=host \
vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 \
--model mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \
--tensor-parallel-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser mistral \
--reasoning-parser mistral \
--enable-auto-tool-choice \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85
Key parameter notes:
--tool-call-parser mistral
and
--reasoning-parser mistral
: required for tool usage and to separate reasoning from content in responses.
If you run short of GPU memory, lower
--max-model-len
and/or
--max-num-seqs
(concurrency). See the
vLLM guide on conserving memory
.

Speculative decoding (DSpark)
The checkpoint ships a DSpark draft head next to the target weights: 3 dense MLA draft layers in BF16 that propose a block of 3 tokens with a recurrent Markov head.
To enable it, add the following argument to the serving command above:
--speculative-config
'{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}'
num_speculative_tokens
is set to 3, the depth of the draft block.
DSpark speeds up decoding without changing the target model's outputs: we measured up to
1.9x
higher throughput than serving the target model alone. Actual gains depend on hardware and workload.
SGLang
Serve Mistral Large 4 with the
SGLang library
for production-ready inference. See also SGLang's
cookbook
.
Installation
Use the official SGLang Docker image, which includes support for Mistral Large 4:
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:mistral-large-4
Serve the Model
sglang serve \
--model-path mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \
--tp-size 8 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
--max-running-requests 64 \
--reasoning-parser auto \
--tool-call-parser auto \
--host 0.0.0.0 \
--port 30000
Speculative decoding (DSpark) is on and this recipe pins
--max-running-requests
to
64
. Adjust it to match your target concurrency — if you remove the flag, SGLang falls back to
48
.
Key parameter notes:
--speculative-algorithm DSPARK
: enables the embedded DSpark draft head, which proposes blocks of 3 tokens. Remove this flag to serve without speculation.
--tp-size 8
: example tensor-parallel size for a node of 8 GPUs; adjust to your topology.
--reasoning-parser auto
and
--tool-call-parser auto
: let SGLang pick the reasoning and tool-call parsers for this model.

capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe.¦Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union.¦Find more information on our¦blog¦. The model is also served on the¦Mistral API¦as¦mistral-large-4¦.¦The checkpoint ships with an embedded DSpark speculative decoding draft head — see¦Speculative decoding (DSpark)¦.¦A quantized¦NVFP4 checkpoint¦is also available, with a smaller memory footprint, faster inference and same performance. It targets Blackwell GPUs and supports vLLM and SGLang.¦Key Features¦Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices:¦~1T total / ~52B active parameters¦: granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert.¦1M context length¦, for long-context workloads.¦Multimodal input¦: accepts text and image input, with text output. Pixtral-style vision encoder trained to handle variable image sizes and aspect ratios.¦Instruct and Reasoning functionalities¦with function calls, reasoning effort configurable per request.¦Mistral Large 4 offers the following capabilities:¦Reasoning Mode¦: three reasoning efforts —¦low¦,¦medium¦,¦high¦(default) — so the same model can answer a quick chat reply or work through a complex agentic run.¦Vision¦: analyzes images, charts, technical drawings, and documents, with state-of-the-art visual grounding among open weights.¦Multilingual¦: natively fluent in 160+ languages, including all official languages of the European Union.¦System Prompt¦: strong adherence and support for system prompts.¦Agentic¦: native function calling, JSON output, and strict JSON schema enforcement.¦Cybersecurity¦: state of the art among open-weight models for security work, while refusing malicious requests.¦Large Context Window¦: supports a 1M context window.¦We release this model under the¦Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License¦: a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral.¦Recommended Settings¦Reasoning Effort¦:¦'low'¦/¦'medium'¦/¦'high'¦— default is¦'high'¦.¦Use¦reasoning_effort="high"¦for complex prompts and agentic usage,¦'low'¦for fast chat replies and¦'medium'¦for day to day usage.¦Sampling¦: for all reasoning efforts, we recommend the following sampling parameters:¦temperature=1.0¦top_p=0.95¦System Prompt¦: define a clear environment and use case, including guidance on how to effectively leverage tools in agentic systems.¦Tools¦: keep the set of tools well-defined and limit their number to the minimum required for the use case.¦Context¦: the checkpoint supports a 1M context window.¦Benchmarks¦We compared Mistral Large 4 with recent open-weight models. We report results on agentic coding and global intelligence here; for more benchmarks, especially on cybersecurity, finance and law, see our¦blog post¦.¦Agentic Coding¦Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.¦On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, ML4 scores¦48%¦, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using¦47%¦fewer tokens per task on average.¦Global Intelligence¦On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, Mistral Large 4 scores¦26¦, the highest among western open-weight models. Cybersecurity AI Knowledge Base — PhD-Level Dataset
Overview
This is the most comprehensive cybersecurity knowledge base ever assembled for AI training. It covers
all domains
of cybersecurity at
PhD-level depth
— from offensive red teaming and bug bounty exploitation to defensive SOC operations, digital forensics, and cutting-edge AI/LLM security.
Size:
16 GB |
Files:
507 |
Domains:
30+ |
Sources:
15+ platforms
Purpose
Train the world's most capable cybersecurity AI assistant
Cover every domain: offensive, defensive, forensics, compliance, AI security
Include real-world attack/defend/detect/analyze methodologies
Provide hands-on lab scenarios from HackTheBox, TryHackMe, PortSwigger, VulnHub
Reference MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP, NIST, CIS frameworks
No restrictions — full offensive and defensive coverage for security research

] =

"

i
in
range
(N):

(

{i +
1
}
/
{N}
] Requesting completion..."
, flush=
True
)

15
,
120

402

0

]

(

{i +
1

/

]
{elapsed:
.1
f}
s:

, flush=
True
)
print
(

{
len
(texts)}
samples."
, flush=
True
)
return
texts

:

China A-Share Level-2 Archive
2017–2026 · Quotes, orders and trades · Parquet
A historical archive of Chinese exchange Level-2 data, supplied through a vendor export.
It includes ten-level quote snapshots, individual order messages and trade-stream records.
The files cover A-share stocks
and non-stock instruments
such as ETFs and bonds.
“Full-market” describes the export's scope, not a guarantee that every instrument or message is present.

Innovating with machine learning on AWS
On AWS, you can access performant infrastructure, deployment resources, data governance solutions, and
AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs)
with optimized open source frameworks, so that you can focus on your machine learning tasks.
Build and Scale AI/ML on AWS
AWS offers a comprehensive suite of AI/ML tools and services supporting every stage of the machine learning lifecycle.
Amazon SageMaker AI
provides fully managed end-to-end model development and deployment, with
SageMaker HyperPod
enabling distributed training at scale featuring
checkpointless recovery
and elastic scaling.
Amazon Bedrock
enables building generative AI and agentic applications with leading foundation models including the
Amazon Nova family
(Nova 2 Sonic, Nova 2 Lite, Nova 2 Omni, Nova Act, and Nova Forge). Bedrock
AgentCore
rovides policy controls, quality evaluations, and enhanced memory for deploying trusted AI agents, while the open source while the open source
Strands Agents SDK
simplifies agent orchestration. Train your own models or fine-tune open source models cost-effectively using the new
Trainium3 UltraServers
powered by AWS's first 3nm AI chip. AWS custom AI accelerators also include
Inferentia
for low-latency inference and
Graviton5
for best-in-class price performance. Whether you're building large language models, generative AI, AI agents, or computer vision applications—scaling on AWS is easy.
Learn more about these services and others:
AWS GPUs for Machine Learning
AWS Deep Learning AMIs
Artificial Intelligence on AWS
Building AI Agents with Strands Agents SDK
AWS offers
Strands Agents
, an open source SDK that simplifies the development and deployment of AI agents. Supporting models from Amazon Bedrock, Meta's Llama, and other providers — Strands Agents enables developers to build production ready multi-agent systems with minimal code.
Introduction to Strands Agents Blog
Strands Agents on GitHub
AWS & Hugging Face Collaboration
AWS and Hugging Face are working together to simplify and accelerate the adoption of advanced machine learning models. This
collaboration
offers streamlined training using Hugging Face Deep Learning Containers with SageMaker AI distributed training libraries, simplifying workflows with the SageMaker AI Python SDK for efficient model training. Deployment is made effortless through the Hugging Face Inference toolkit and DLCs, allowing users to deploy trained models on the Hugging Face Hub. Amazon SageMaker AI facilitates the creation of scalable endpoints with built-in monitoring and enterprise-level security. This joint effort empowers teams to move quickly from experimentation to production, leveraging cutting-edge models and scalable infrastructure to drive innovation in machine learning projects.

GenAI SW Catalogue
Choose from a broad range of solutions designed to simplify and accelerate your AI development timeline, from training and optimization to deployment.
Chat Q & A Solution
Intel® AI for Enterprise RAG Chat Q&A builds upon the strong foundation of OPEA. It extends this base with key features that enhance security, scalability, performance and user experience.
Content Summarization Solution
Intel® AI for Enterprise RAG Document Summarization solution builds upon the strong foundation of OPEA. Summarizes large documents or datasets, providing concise and relevant insights quickly.
Audio Q & A Solution
Intel® AI for Enterprise RAG AudioQnA solution builds upon the strong foundation of OPEA. Enables seamless voice-based interactions, allowing large language models (LLMs) to engage in dynamic conversations with users.
Inference as a Service
Intel® AI for Enterprise Inference is aimed to streamline and enhance the deployment and management of AI inference services on Intel hardware.
Code Translation
Automates code translation from one programming language to another to help maintain code efficiency and reduce human error in an enterprise setting.
Code Generation Solution
A specialized AI model designed to generate high-quality computer code, accelerating the development process with greater efficiency.
Visual Q & A Solution
Answers open-ended questions by interpreting visual data, allowing AI to understand and respond to queries about images.
FAQ Generation Solution
Generates frequently asked questions (FAQs) from various data types with optimized performance, security and scalability for thousands of users.

Transformers
Transformers acts as the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, computer
vision, audio, video, and multimodal models, for both inference and training.
It centralizes the model definition so that this definition is agreed upon across the ecosystem.
transformers
is the
pivot across frameworks: if a model definition is supported, it will be compatible with the majority of training
frameworks (Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, …), inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, …),
and adjacent modeling libraries (llama.cpp, mlx, …) which leverage the model definition from
transformers
.
We pledge to help support new state-of-the-art models and democratize their usage by having their model definition be
simple, customizable, and efficient.
There are over 1M+ Transformers
model checkpoints
on the
Hugging Face Hub
you can use.
Explore the
Hub
today to find a model and use Transformers to help you get started right away.
Explore the
Models Timeline
to discover the latest text, vision, audio and multimodal model architectures in Transformers.
Features
Transformers provides everything you need for inference or training with state-of-the-art pretrained models. Some of the main features include:
Pipeline
: Simple and optimized inference class for many machine learning tasks like text generation, image segmentation, automatic speech recognition, document question answering, and more.
Trainer
: A comprehensive trainer that supports features such as mixed precision, torch.compile, and FlashAttention for training and distributed training for PyTorch models.
generate
: Fast text generation with large language models (LLMs) and vision language models (VLMs), including support for streaming and multiple decoding strategies.
Design
Read our
Philosophy
to learn more about Transformers’ design principles.
Transformers is designed for developers and machine learning engineers and researchers. Its main design principles are:
Fast and easy to use: Every model is implemented from only three main classes (configuration, model, and preprocessor) and can be quickly used for inference or training with
Pipeline
or
Trainer
.
Pretrained models: Reduce your carbon footprint, compute cost and time by using a pretrained model instead of training an entirely new one. Each pretrained model is reproduced as closely as possible to the original model and offers state-of-the-art performance.
Learn
If you’re new to Transformers or want to learn more about transformer models, we recommend starting with the
LLM course
. This comprehensive course covers everything from the fundamentals of how transformer models work to practical applications across various tasks. You’ll learn the complete workflow, from curating high-quality datasets to fine-tuning large language models and implementing reasoning capabilities. The course contains both theoretical and hands-on exercises to build a solid foundational knowledge of transformer models as you learn.

Diffusers
Diffusers provides pretrained diffusion models and the building blocks for custom image, video, and audio workflows.
It has two main paths.
DiffusionPipeline
supports few-line inference with pretrained checkpoints, plus adapters like LoRA. This is the easy path for generation.
Modular Diffusers
enables composable blocks and
ModularPipeline
for custom pipelines when you need more control.
Optimizations such as offloading and quantization keep large models runnable on memory-constrained devices. If memory is not an issue, Diffusers also supports
torch.compile
for faster inference.
Browse trending Diffusers models on the
Hub
now.
Learn
If you’re a beginner, start with the
Hugging Face Diffusion Models Course
. It covers diffusion theory and how to generate images, fine-tune models, and more with Diffusers.
The
Quickstart
also includes a copyable agent setup prompt for inference.

Safetensors
Safetensors is a new simple format for storing tensors safely (as opposed to pickle) and that is still fast (zero-copy). Safetensors is really
fast 🚀
.
Installation
with pip:
Copied
pip
install
safetensors
with conda:
Copied
conda
install
-c conda-forge safetensors
Usage
Load tensors
Copied
from
safetensors
import
safe_open
tensors = {}
with
safe_open(
"model.safetensors"
, framework=
"pt"
, device=
0
)
as
f:
for
k
in
f.keys():
tensors[k] = f.get_tensor(k)
Loading only part of the tensors (interesting when running on multiple GPU)
Copied
from
safetensors
import
safe_open
tensors = {}
with
safe_open(
"model.safetensors"
, framework=
"pt"
, device=
0
)
as
f:
tensor_slice = f.get_slice(
"embedding"
)
vocab_size, hidden_dim = tensor_slice.get_shape()
tensor = tensor_slice[:, :hidden_dim]
Save tensors
Copied
import
torch
from
safetensors.torch
import
save_file
tensors = {
"embedding"
: torch.zeros((
2
,
2
)),
"attention"
: torch.zeros((
2
,
3
))
}
save_file(tensors,
"model.safetensors"
)

🤗 Hub client library
The
huggingface_hub
library allows you to interact with the
Hugging Face
Hub
, a machine learning platform for creators and collaborators.
Discover pre-trained models and datasets for your projects or play with the hundreds of
machine learning apps hosted on the Hub. You can also create and share your own models
and datasets with the community. The
huggingface_hub
library provides a simple way to
do all these things with Python.
Read the
quick start guide
to get up and running with the
huggingface_hub
library. You will learn how to download files from the Hub, create a
repository, and upload files to the Hub. Keep reading to learn more about how to manage
your repositories on the 🤗 Hub, how to interact in discussions or even how to run inference.
How-to guides
Practical guides to help you achieve a specific goal. Take a look at these guides to learn how to use huggingface_hub to solve real-world problems.
Reference
Exhaustive and technical description of huggingface_hub classes and methods.
Conceptual guides
High-level explanations for building a better understanding of huggingface_hub philosophy.
Contribute
All contributions to the
huggingface_hub
are welcomed and equally valued! 🤗 Besides
adding or fixing existing issues in the code, you can also help improve the
documentation by making sure it is accurate and up-to-date, help answer questions on
issues, and request new features you think will improve the library. Take a look at the
contribution
guide
to
learn more about how to submit a new issue or feature request, how to submit a pull
request, and how to test your contributions to make sure everything works as expected.
Contributors should also be respectful of our
code of
conduct
to
create an inclusive and welcoming collaborative space for everyone.

TRL - Transformers Reinforcement Learning
TRL is a full stack library where we provide a set of tools to train transformer language models with methods like Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), Reward Modeling, and more.
The library is integrated with 🤗
transformers
.
🎉 What’s New
🔥 Mistral Large 4:
Fine-tune
Mistral Large 4
with
SFTTrainer
on a single node of 8 B300s, on top of its FP8 weights. See the
LoRA example
.
🚀 Training on AMD GPUs:
TRL’s trainers now run on
AMD Instinct GPUs
through PyTorch’s ROCm build.
🔥 Beam:
Fine-tune
Beam
with
SFTTrainer
on a single node of 8 B300s. See the
LoRA example
.
🔥 Muse Spark Open:
Fine-tune
Muse Spark Open
with
SFTTrainer
, sharded across your GPUs at load time. See the
8-node LoRA example
.
🚀 Training on AWS Trainium:
TRL’s trainers now run on
AWS Trainium
through TorchNeuron, PyTorch’s native Neuron backend.

smolagents
What is smolagents?
smolagents
is an open-source Python library designed to make it extremely easy to build and run agents using just a few lines of code.
Key features of
smolagents
include:
✨
Simplicity
: The logic for agents fits in ~thousand lines of code. We kept abstractions to their minimal shape above raw code!
🧑‍💻
First-class support for Code Agents
:
CodeAgent
writes its actions in code (as opposed to “agents being used to write code”) to invoke tools or perform computations, enabling natural composability (function nesting, loops, conditionals). To make it secure, we support
executing in sandboxed environment
via
Modal
,
Blaxel
,
E2B
, or Docker.
📡
Common Tool-Calling Agent Support
: In addition to CodeAgents,
ToolCallingAgent
supports usual JSON/text-based tool-calling for scenarios where that paradigm is preferred.
🤗
Hub integrations
: Seamlessly share and load agents and tools to/from the Hub as Gradio Spaces.
🌐
Model-agnostic
: Easily integrate any large language model (LLM), whether it’s hosted on the Hub via
Inference providers
, accessed via APIs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or many others via LiteLLM integration, or run locally using Transformers or Ollama. Powering an agent with your preferred LLM is straightforward and flexible.
👁️
Modality-agnostic
: Beyond text, agents can handle vision, video, and audio inputs, broadening the range of possible applications. Check out
this tutorial
for vision.
🛠️
Tool-agnostic
: You can use tools from any
MCP server
, from
LangChain
, you can even use a
Hub Space
as a tool.
💻
CLI Tools
: Comes with command-line utilities (smolagent, webagent) for quickly running agents without writing boilerplate code.
Quickstart
Get started with smolagents in just a few minutes! This guide will show you how to create and run your first agent.
Installation
Install smolagents with pip:
Copied
pip install
'smolagents[toolkit]'
# Includes default tools like web search
Create Your First Agent
Here’s a minimal example to create and run an agent:
Copied
from
smolagents
import
CodeAgent, InferenceClientModel
# Initialize a model (using Hugging Face Inference API)
model = InferenceClientModel()
# Uses a default model
# Create an agent with no tools
agent = CodeAgent(tools=[], model=model)
# Run the agent with a task
result = agent.run(
"Calculate the sum of numbers from 1 to 10"
)
print
(result)
That’s it! Your agent will use Python code to solve the task and return the result.
Adding Tools
Let’s make our agent more capable by adding some tools:
Copied
from
smolagents
import
CodeAgent, InferenceClientModel, DuckDuckGoSearchTool
model = InferenceClientModel()
agent = CodeAgent(
tools=[DuckDuckGoSearchTool()],
model=model,
)
# Now the agent can search the web!
result = agent.run(
"What is the current weather in Paris?"
)
print
(result)
Using Different Models
You can use various models with your agent:
Copied
# Using a specific model from Hugging Face
model = InferenceClientModel(model_id=
"meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf"
)
# Using OpenAI/Anthropic (requires 'smolagents[litellm]')
from
smolagents
import

PEFT
🤗 PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) is a library for efficiently adapting large pretrained models to various downstream applications without fine-tuning all of a model’s parameters because it is prohibitively costly. PEFT methods only fine-tune a small number of (extra) model parameters - significantly decreasing computational and storage costs - while yielding performance comparable to a fully fine-tuned model. This makes it more accessible to train and store large language models (LLMs) and other big models on consumer hardware.
PEFT is integrated with the Transformers, Diffusers, and Accelerate libraries to provide a faster and easier way to load, train, and use large models for inference.
There are numerous methods to "adapt" existing models, often extensively integrating into the model. PEFT can be thought of as a framework for arbitrary methods of model adaption (modifying weights, wrapping layers, manipulating KV-caches, ...) while also serving as a reference implementation for many fine-tuning methods.

Load a dataset in a single line of code, and use our powerful data processing and streaming methods to quickly get your dataset ready for training in a deep learning model. , allowing you to easily load and share a dataset with the wider machine learning community.

text-generation-inference is now in maintenance mode. Going forward, we will accept pull requests for minor bug fixes, documentation improvements and lightweight maintenance tasks.
TGI has initiated the movement for optimized inference engines to rely on a
transformers
model architectures. This approach is now adopted by downstream inference engines, which we contribute to and recommend using going forward:
vllm
,
SGLang
, as well as local engines with inter-compatibility such as llama.cpp or MLX.
Text Generation Inference (TGI) is a toolkit for deploying and serving Large Language Models (LLMs). TGI enables high-performance text generation for the most popular open-source LLMs, including Llama, Falcon, StarCoder, BLOOM, GPT-NeoX, and T5.
Text Generation Inference implements many optimizations and features, such as:
Simple launcher to serve most popular LLMs
Production ready (distributed tracing with Open Telemetry, Prometheus metrics)
Tensor Parallelism for faster inference on multiple GPUs
Token streaming using Server-Sent Events (SSE)
Continuous batching of incoming requests for increased total throughput
Optimized transformers code for inference using
Flash Attention
and
Paged Attention
on the most popular architectures
Quantization with
bitsandbytes
and
GPT-Q
Safetensors
weight loading
Watermarking with
A Watermark for Large Language Models
Logits warper (temperature scaling, top-p, top-k, repetition penalty)
Stop sequences
Log probabilities
Fine-tuning Support: Utilize fine-tuned models for specific tasks to achieve higher accuracy and performance.
Guidance
: Enable function calling and tool-use by forcing the model to generate structured outputs based on your own predefined output schemas.
Text Generation Inference is used in production by multiple projects, such as:
Hugging Chat
, an open-source interface for open-access models, such as Open Assistant and Llama
OpenAssistant
, an open-source community effort to train LLMs in the open
nat.dev
, a playground to explore and compare LLMs.

Accelerate
Accelerate is a library that enables the same PyTorch code to be run across any distributed configuration by adding just four lines of code! In short, training and inference at scale made simple, efficient and adaptable.
Copied
+ from accelerate import Accelerator
+ accelerator = Accelerator()
+ model, optimizer, training_dataloader, scheduler = accelerator.prepare(
+     model, optimizer, training_dataloader, scheduler
+ )
for batch in training_dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
inputs, targets = batch
inputs = inputs.to(device)
targets = targets.to(device)
outputs = model(inputs)
loss = loss_function(outputs, targets)
+     accelerator.backward(loss)
optimizer.step()
scheduler.step()
Built on
torch_xla
and
torch.distributed
, Accelerate takes care of the heavy lifting, so you don’t have to write any custom code to adapt to these platforms.
Convert existing codebases to utilize
DeepSpeed
, perform
fully sharded data parallelism
, and have automatic support for mixed-precision training!
To get a better idea of this process, make sure to check out the
Tutorials
!
This code can then be launched on any system through Accelerate’s CLI interface:
Copied
accelerate launch {my_script.py}

Upvote
105
+100
The tensor viewer now loads much faster on large sharded models. When you open a model's
model.safetensors.index.json
, the Hub sends the headers of all shards in a single request, so your browser no longer fetches each shard one by one. For example,
DeepSeek-V3.2
now loads in 0.45s instead of 9.2s,
GLM-5.3
in 0.57s instead of 4.0s, and
Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct
in 0.27s instead of 1.2s.

Hugging Face Privacy Policy
🗓 Effective Date: March 28, 2023
We have implemented this Privacy Policy because your privacy is important to us. This Privacy Policy (the “Policy”) describes the type of information that Hugging Face, Inc. (the “Company”) gathers from users of the Hugging Face services (the “Services”), and how the Company uses that information.
The Policy is part of the Company Terms of Use. The Policy applies to all users of the Services (“Users”).
The Company occasionally collects Personal Information from Users. “Personal Information” means any information that can, alone or associated with other information, be used to identify an individual, for instance by reference of a name, a username, an email address, an IP address, a photograph or others.
By using the Services, you consent to the terms of the Policy and to our processing of Personal Information in the manner and for the purposes set forth herein. If you do not agree with the Policy, please do not use the Services.
The Company reserves the right, at its sole discretion, to change the Policy at any time, which change will be effective 10 days following posting the revision to the Policy on the Hugging Face website (the “Website”). Your continued use of the Services 10 days following such posting means you accept those changes.
1. INFORMATION WE COLLECT
The Company collects the following information, some of which might be Personal Information.
A. Information you provide directly
The Company collects information directly provided by Users as part of using the Services, such as:
information provided as part of setting up an account on the Website: email address, password, username, full name, and other optional information such as an avatar, your interests, or usernames to your third-party social networks,
payment information provided, if you decide to upgrade your user or organization account: credit card information,
other information and materials that you decide to post on the Website (e.g., the discussion forum, or other),
communications between you and the Company, as part of using the Services.
At any time during your use of the Services, you may decide to share some information or content publicly or privately.
If you decide to share your information or content publicly, and if you decide to include Personal Information, you understand that anyone may view this information.
If you decide to keep your information private and control the access to it, you understand that only the users that you authorize will view this information. The Company also reserves the right to access this information with your consent, or without your consent only for the purposes of pursuing legitimate interests such as maintaining security on its Services or complying with any legal or regulatory obligations.
B. Information we collect from third parties
We may collect Information from third parties that help us deliver the Services or process information.
C. Information we automatically collect from your use of the Services
The Company automatically records information from your use of the Services such as:
information about your Use of the Services, your session (date, location), your IP address,
information from cookies, especially your login information, your preferences,
information about your device: type, model, version, operating system, browser
D. Cookies
We use cookies only for the purposes of delivering, updating, monitoring, improving the Services, and maintaining security on our Services by detecting, preventing and responding to any type of threats or incidents.
We may collect Information through those cookies. If you do not wish to accept these cookies and you decide to disable them, you will not be able to access and use the Services.
E. “Do Not Track”
On September 27, 2013, California enacted A.B. 370, amending the California Online Privacy Protection Act to require website operators to disclose how they respond to "Do Not Track Signals"; and whether third parties collect personally identifiable information about users when they use online services.
The Company honors "do not track" signals and does not track, use cookies, or use advertising when a “do not track” mechanism is in place.
The Company does not authorize the collection of personally identifiable information from our users for third party use through advertising technologies without separate member consent.
California Civil Code Section 1798.83 also permits customers who are California residents to request certain information regarding Our disclosure of Personal Information to third parties for direct marketing purposes. To make such a request, please send an email to
privacy@huggingface.co
. Please note that the Company is only required to respond to one request per customer each year.

to operate and improve the Services by providing you with more effective customer service, making the Services easier to use by eliminating the need for you to enter the same information repeatedly; performing research and analysis aimed at improving the Services, or other products and technologies of the Company; automatically updating the Services; diagnosing or fixing problems with the Services,

arXiv Complete Corpus
A snapshot of arXiv's metadata, version history, submission files and rendered
documents. It covers 3,148,796 papers and includes file contents, paths, sizes
and SHA-256 digests. Metadata comes from arXiv's OAI-PMH
arXivRaw
interface;
files come from the GCS mirror, S3 source archives and direct PDF fetches.
This release holds a PDF for 99.47% of papers and 99.54% of versions reported
with a non-zero submission size. It is a one-off snapshot; coverage gaps are
documented below.

The main limits to account for are:
paper_text
retains LaTeX syntax, comments and macros. It includes
withdrawal stubs and some incorrectly selected templates; it needs filtering
before use as a training corpus.
Source packages are unversioned. A paper's newest held PDF can be older than
the newest version arXiv reports.
Large binary rows and row groups require substantial memory. Early exit
from
datasets
streams also failed on the versions tested for this release.
The
html
family is indexed in
files
but has no content config.
Licences vary by paper. The compilation's CC0 dedication does not apply to
the papers; see

Requests and outcomes
The pass targeted 10,085 version pairs missing a PDF on 2026-08-30. Each
was requested from
/pdf/
, the path arXiv's
robots.txt
explicitly allows,
from a single host behind a global rate limiter that doubles its interval on any
throttle signal.
Only the first 289 went at the fifteen-second
Crawl-delay
that file declares; the remaining 9,796 went at a 1.20-second global interval —
0.83 requests a second, 12.5× the rate arXiv publishes.
arXiv signalled
throttling zero times in 10,224 requests, but the faster rate was our choice
and it is recorded here rather than left out. Every non-success was requested

Verifying your download
SHA256SUMS
at the repository root lists every Parquet file. From a complete
download's root directory:
sha256sum
-c SHA256SUMS
For a filtered download, with the manifest available in the same root:

The latter checks only files that are present; it does not certify that the
requested subset is complete. File checksums verify transfer integrity,
while row-level digests verify the content inside Parquet.

Welcome to SimReady Central
SimReady Central is in Alpha. We are accepting contributors through the
Community tab
.
SimReady Central connects creators and users of simulation-ready digital twins for Physical AI. It helps robotics researchers, simulation engineers, and application developers discover assets for training, testing, and industrial planning.
Contributors host and version their asset packages in their own Hugging Face datasets. SimReady Central provides a shared index of reviewed contributions. You retain ownership of your assets and control their releases and licenses.
SimReady assets combine OpenUSD content with simulation metadata and validation evidence for a defined use case.
Read the SimReady Central documentation
for the full workflow, requirements, and resources.

Dataset Description
This dataset contains 10,000 agentic coding and reasoning multi-turn high-quality traces generated by the new Fable 5.1 model using max reasoning effort.
It holds almost 500,000,000 tokens of step-by-step chain-of-thought programming across multiple complex domains.
It has also been deduplicated and
heavily
filtered to remove low-quality traces, keeping only high-quality traces.

Dataset Contents & Coverage
The dataset includes step-by-step problem-solving for complex coding tasks, including:
Algorithm design, implementation, and performance optimization.
Advanced debugging and error-handling.
Multi-step logic design and compliance with complex prompt constraints.
Uses
Distilling Fable 5.1 agentic coding and reasoning capabilities down to smaller LLMs.
Improve general coding and reasoning quality.
Teaching models to generate clear chain-of-thought steps and tool-use before outputting their final answer.

Granary-v2: Multilingual Speech Recognition, Translation and Instruction Data
Granary-v2
is NVIDIA's second release of generated labels and instruction pairs
for multilingual speech. It re-processes a broad set of source corpora through
an entirely new labelling pipeline that produces not just transcripts and translations, but
inverse text normalization, captioning, code-switching and speech-QA targets, plus
ready-to-train instruction pairs.
The pipeline source is already public.
All of it lives in
NeMo Curator
.
The full end-to-end runs and the per-stage scripts will follow soon.

in the Common
Voice 26.0 release. Fetch a corpus from its own distributor, then join on that
suffix.
