Repository Structure
nvidia/Granary-v2/
└── <language>/                 # ISO 639-1 codes
└── <corpus>/
└── <lang>_asr.jsonl.gz
One or more manifest files per (language, corpus). Large manifests can be split into shards.
Unlike Granary-v1, there is no separate
<lang>_ast-en.jsonl
: every translation travels
inline in each record's
translations
field, alongside its quality-estimation score. The
manifest files for each (language, corpus) carry both the ASR and the AST targets.
translations
is keyed by target language, and the release runs in
both directions
.
Non-English audio is translated into English, which is the
AST (X→en) h
column. English
audio is translated the other way, into 31 targets at once (
ar
,
bg
,
cs
,
da
,
de
,
el
,
es
,
et
,
fi
,
fr
,
he
,
hi
,
hr
,
hu
,
it
,
ja
,
ko
,
lt
,
lv
,
mt
,
nl
,
pl
,
pt
,
ro
,
ru
,
sk
,
sl
,
sv
,
th
,
uk
,
zh
) — that is the
AST (en→X) h
column, and it is why corpora like LibriLight and VCTK show no X→English
hours yet still carry translation.
Coverage is per-record, and a present key is
not
a usable translation: the pipeline
writes a stub with an empty
translation_raw
where its quality estimator rejected the
candidate.
Test
translation_raw
for non-emptiness
rather than assuming a key means
a translation. Both table columns count distinct audio, once per record however many
targets it carries, so neither double-counts and the two never sum past a corpus's hours.

SimReady GLB
Open the 3D viewer
to search all 2,595 models and
orbit any of them in the browser.
Web-ready glTF binary (
.glb
) copies of the 3D models in
nvidia/simready-assets
. Each file loads directly in
three.js, Babylon.js, model-viewer or any glTF 2.0 viewer.
Models by NVIDIA SimReady, licensed CC BY 4.0. This dataset converts and compresses them. It does not change what
they show. If you use these files, credit NVIDIA as the original author and link the source dataset.

Example: the V8 engine (
engineAssembly_v8_engine_a01
) is an 888 MB glb out of Blender and
7.4 MB here. Its first frame in Chrome took 9.4 s before and 0.57 s after.
What is in it
glb/<asset>.glb
: one file per SimReady asset folder, named like the folder in the source dataset.
thumbs/<asset>.webp
: a 512 px render of each glb, with
thumbs/metadata.jsonl
holding its category, size,
triangles and draw calls. The Dataset Viewer above shows this table.
manifest.jsonl
: one line per asset with size, triangles, draw calls and textures before and after optimization,
plus the number of hulls, concave parts and drives.
newton_loader/
: the loader for NVIDIA Newton.
Download
All files, about 3.2 GB:
hf download codepawl/simready-glb --repo-type dataset --local-dir simready-glb
One category, for example every food model:
hf download codepawl/simready-glb --repo-type dataset --include
"glb/food_*"
--local-dir simready-glb
One file from Python:
from
huggingface_hub
import
hf_hub_download
path = hf_hub_download(
"codepawl/simready-glb"
,
"glb/engineAssembly_v8_engine_a01.glb"
, repo_type=
"dataset"
)
Loading in three.js

Physics and moving parts
2,587 files carry the rigid bodies, mass and physics materials of their SimReady USD. 929 of
them also carry joints, 5,550 in all: door hinges, drawer slides, buttons, wheels and lids. Each file holds
this data in two forms:
KHR_physics_rigid_bodies
, the Khronos glTF physics extension. Each part has a
motion
with its mass, center of
mass and inertia. Each mesh has a convex hull
collider
with friction and restitution. Each joint has its limits.
Loaders that do not read the extension ignore it.
Plain node extras, which three.js puts in
object.userData
. A moving part has
joints: [{ type, parent, pivot, axis, min, max, unit }]
, with the pivot and axis in model space at rest.
Revolute limits are in degrees and prismatic limits are in meters. Parts also have
mass
in kg and
density
in
kg/m³.

Simulating in NVIDIA Newton
Each file with physics data also carries the data that a simulator needs and a viewer does not:
17,507 collision hulls in
extras.collisionHulls
of each body node. 2,852 of the 8,496 parts are concave.
A concave part gets up to 8 hulls, so a cabinet or a bin stays hollow. A hull has at most 48 points, or 32 in a concave part.
2,145 joint drives in 333 files, in the
drives
array of the joint in
KHR_physics_rigid_bodies
.
Inertia of 256 small parts in 67 files, which the earlier rounding had set to zero.
These additions make the set 0.17% larger: 3,180.2 MB to 3,185.5 MB, with a median file of 0.416 MB. Meshes, materials and
textures are byte-identical to the earlier files in all 2,595 files. The hulls sit after the old binary data, so
existing loaders read the files as before.
Half of the files have hulls within 3.9 mm of the part's own convex shape. The figure is 12 mm at the 95th percentile
and 177 mm in the worst file. A hull side that is nearly flat along an axis is then made exactly flat, which moves its
points outward by up to 2 cm. Newton's contact code turns an uneven bottom into false depth, which kicks the part upward.

How the files were made
Download
simready_usd/
from each asset folder.
source_assets/
is skipped because it holds a second copy of
the textures for MDL shaders.
Check that
.metadata/LICENSE.txt
is CC BY 4.0.
Import the USD in Blender 5.2 and remove the collision, proxy and grasp helper prims. Export a glb with the
original textures.
Optimize with glTF Transform 4.5. Remove the USD instance prototypes Blender brings in next to the placed parts,
remove duplicate mesh instances, then dedup, prune and weld.
Resize textures to 1024 px as WebP. Compress geometry with meshopt at its high level
(
EXT_meshopt_compression
with octahedral normals and quantized attributes).
Read the rigid bodies, mass, physics materials and joints from the USD layers and write them into the glb JSON.
The USD is Z-up, so joint frames and axes are turned to the glb's Y-up.
Cut each concave part into convex pieces and keep the hull points that stick out most. Make nearly flat hull sides
exactly flat. Read the drives and the full inertia from the USD. Append the hulls after the binary data.
Assets with UDIM textures have each tile split into its own material before the export, with its UVs moved into 0-1.
Blender's own UDIM handling in the glTF exporter drops the faces of some tiles.
No mesh simplification is applied. The triangle drop comes from removed duplicates and helper geometry.
The conversion scripts are in
codepawl/3d-builds
.
Known gaps
SimReady collides with signed distance fields built from each render mesh. The
collider
of each mesh in
KHR_physics_rigid_bodies
stays one convex hull, which every engine can build, so hollow parts collide as if filled
there. Use
extras.collisionHulls
to keep them hollow.
KHR_physics_rigid_bodies
is still a Khronos review draft, so
check that your engine reads it. The node extras work with any loader. USD simulation settings are not carried
over. Materials are converted to glTF PBR, so MDL-only shader effects are lost.
In Newton, parts of one file do not collide with each other, because SimReady's overlapping parts jam their hinges
otherwise. Nothing latches a door or a drawer, so use a drive to hold them closed. Two sample files do not stay still:
electrical_power_terminal_a01
is 5.1 m tall and 0.52 m deep, and it falls over when it stands free. Load it with
fixed_base=True
.
paint_supplies_brush_a05
, a 44 g brush, still rocks after 9 s. With
rigid_contact_relaxation=0.2
it settles in 9 s.
Inertia differs from the USD where the loader raises it to its floor. Only 43 of the 2,595 files had these simulation
checks, so other files can have the same problems.
Two joints in the USD are left out because they hold nothing: the fixed joint of
ladder_multiPurpose_aluminium_a05
points at a part with no rigid body, and one fixed joint of
serviceTool_brakeCaliper_pistonWindBackKit_a01
joins a body to itself.

Newton's contact code turns an uneven bottom into false depth, which kicks the part upward.¦newton_loader/simready_newton¦adds a file to a Newton model. It needs Newton 1.7, SciPy and meshoptimizer.¦import¦newton¦import¦newton.solvers¦from¦simready_newton¦import¦add_simready_glb¦builder = newton.ModelBuilder(up_axis=newton.Axis.Y)¦builder.add_ground_plane()¦add_simready_glb(builder,¦"glb/bin_waste_a01.glb"¦, position=(¦0.0¦,¦0.5¦,¦0.0¦))¦model = builder.finalize()¦solver = newton.solvers.SolverXPBD(model, iterations=¦8¦, joint_linear_relaxation=¦0.3¦, joint_angular_relaxation=¦0.2¦)¦Use these two relaxation values with¦SolverXPBD¦. The default linear value of 0.7 went NaN on¦scaffold_rolling_steel_a03¦within a few frames. The default angular value of 0.4 went NaN on¦climate_shopFan_pedestal_a01¦when every joint was pushed at once. The loader read all 2,595 files with no failures.¦8 files have no rigid bodies, so it adds nothing for them.¦In a file with joints, the loader raises any part's inertia below 1e-4 kg·m² to that value. A part's rotation is slower¦than the source says, and it no longer shakes or goes NaN. Set¦jointed_part_inertia_floor¦to change the value. Files¦with one rigid body use 1e-6 kg·m² (¦inertia_floor¦).¦43 files across the categories were simulated at 60 fps with 8 substeps. 42 of them were compared with their SimReady USD:¦Check¦Result¦Mass, center of mass, joint type, pivot, axis, limits, friction, restitution¦Match¦Dropped from 20 cm stays finite¦43 of 43¦Dropped from 20 cm is at rest after 3 s¦31 of 43¦Dropped from 20 cm is at rest after 9 s (the 12 files left)¦10 of 12¦Every joint pushed at once on a pinned base stays finite¦43 of 43¦At rest means under 0.05 m/s and 0.5 rad/s. The push test stops pushing a free axle above 200 rad/s.¦conveyor_belt_a61¦stayed finite at 400 rad/s and went NaN at 800 rad/s, so keep free axles below that at 480 substeps per second.¦How the files were made¦Download¦simready_usd/¦from each asset folder.¦source_assets/¦is skipped because it holds a second copy of¦the textures for MDL shaders.¦Check that¦.metadata/LICENSE.txt¦is CC BY 4.0.¦Import the USD in Blender 5.2 and remove the collision, proxy and grasp helper prims. Export a glb with the¦original textures.¦Optimize with glTF Transform 4.5. Remove the USD instance prototypes Blender brings in next to the placed parts,¦remove duplicate mesh instances, then dedup, prune and weld.¦Resize textures to 1024 px as WebP. Compress geometry with meshopt at its high level¦(¦EXT_meshopt_compression¦with octahedral normals and quantized attributes).¦Read the rigid bodies, mass, physics materials and joints from the USD layers and write them into the glb JSON.¦The USD is Z-up, so joint frames and axes are turned to the glb's Y-up.¦Cut each concave part into convex pieces and keep the hull points that stick out most. Make nearly flat hull sides¦exactly flat. Read the drives and the full inertia from the USD. Append the hulls after the binary data.¦Assets with UDIM textures have each tile split into its own material before the export, with its UVs moved into 0-1.¦Blender's own UDIM handling in the glTF exporter drops the faces of some tiles.¦No mesh simplification is applied. The triangle drop comes from removed duplicates and helper geometry.¦The conversion scripts are in¦codepawl/3d-builds¦.¦Known gaps¦SimReady collides with signed distance fields built from each render mesh. The¦collider¦of each mesh in¦KHR_physics_rigid_bodies¦stays one convex hull, which every engine can build, so hollow parts collide as if filled¦there. Use¦extras.collisionHulls¦to keep them hollow.¦KHR_physics_rigid_bodies¦is still a Khronos review draft, so¦check that your engine reads it. The node extras work with any loader. USD simulation settings are not carried¦over. Materials are converted to glTF PBR, so MDL-only shader effects are lost.¦In Newton, parts of one file do not collide with each other, because SimReady's overlapping parts jam their hinges¦otherwise. Nothing latches a door or a drawer, so use a drive to hold them closed. Two sample files do not stay still:¦electrical_power_terminal_a01¦is 5.1 m tall and 0.52 m deep, and it falls over when it stands free. Load it with¦fixed_base=True¦.¦paint_supplies_brush_a05¦, a 44 g brush, still rocks after 9 s. With¦rigid_contact_relaxation=0.2¦it settles in 9 s.¦Inertia differs from the USD where the loader raises it to its floor. Only 43 of the 2,595 files had these simulation¦checks, so other files can have the same problems.¦Two joints in the USD are left out because they hold nothing: the fixed joint of¦ladder_multiPurpose_aluminium_a05¦points at a part with no rigid body, and one fixed joint of¦serviceTool_brakeCaliper_pistonWindBackKit_a01¦joins a body to itself.¦Changelog¦2026-11-01: Added collision hulls that keep concave parts hollow, joint drives and the inertia of small parts.¦Added a loader for NVIDIA Newton. BONES-SEED: Skeletal Everyday Embodiment Dataset
BONES-SEED is an open dataset of 142,220 annotated human motion animations for humanoid robotics. It provides motion capture data in
SOMA
and Unitree G1 formats, with natural language descriptions, temporal segmentation, and detailed skeletal metadata.
Project website:
bones.studio/datasets/seed
Interactive viewer:
seed-viewer.bones.studio
Associated code:
github.com/bones-studio/seed-viewer
Total motions
142,220 (71,132 original + 71,088 mirrored)
Total duration
~288 hours (@ 120 fps)
Performers
522 actors (253 F / 269 M)
Age range
17–71 years
Height range
145–199 cm
Weight range
38–145 kg
Output formats
SOMA Uniform · SOMA Proportional · Unitree G1 MuJoCo-compatible
Annotation depth
Up to 6 NL descriptions per motion + temporal segmentation + technical descriptions + skeletal metadata
Intended Uses
BONES-SEED is designed to support research and development in:
Humanoid whole-body control
— training language-conditioned policies for humanoid robots
Motion generation
— text-to-motion and action-to-motion synthesis
Motion retrieval
— natural language search over large motion libraries
Sim-to-real transfer
— leveraging MuJoCo-compatible G1 trajectories for simulation training
Imitation learning
— learning from diverse human demonstrations
Motion understanding
— temporal segmentation, style classification, and activity recognition

Data Formats
Every motion is provided in three skeletal representations supporting two character models:
SOMA
and Unitree G1 robot. SOMA is a canonical body topology and rig that acts as a universal pivot for parametric human body models.
SOMA Proportional (BVH)
A per-actor skeleton that preserves the original performer's body proportions. Each actor has an individual shape file.
soma_proportional/bvh/{date}/{motion_name}.bvh
soma_shapes/soma_proportion_fit_mhr_params/{actor_id}.npz
SOMA Uniform (BVH)
A standardized skeleton shared across all motions, enabling direct comparison and batch processing. Each motion file is paired with a single shared shape file. The base skeleton definition is provided in both BVH and USD formats.
soma_uniform/bvh/{date}/{motion_name}.bvh
soma_shapes/soma_base_fit_mhr_params.npz
soma_shapes/soma_base_rig/soma_base_skel_minimal.bvh
soma_shapes/soma_base_rig/soma_base_skel_minimal.usd
Unitree G1 MuJoCo-compatible (CSV)
Joint-angle trajectories retargeted to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
g1/csv/{date}/{motion_name}.csv
Annotations
Each motion in BONES-SEED comes with rich multimodal annotations designed for language-conditioned policy learning, motion retrieval, and motion generation.

CCORE Three.js 3D Scenes
4,146 high-quality 3D scene examples with prompts, full thinking traces, and complete HTML/JavaScript responses.
The scene code and thinking traces were generated with
MiniMax M3.1 Flash
.
This dataset brings together a broad range of Three.js scenes, from individual objects and detailed interiors to architecture, landscapes, animated mechanisms, and voxel environments. It is intended for training and evaluating models that generate 3D scenes from natural-language instructions.
This dataset was used to train
Qwen3.5-4B-3D-Coder
.

Dataset Description:
This release extends NVIDIA’s existing public
PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles dataset
with additional labels for 1253 specific clips, including:
Metric depth
Per-voxel occupancy, semantic labels, and velocity
These labels are intended to provide target values and labels that can be used to validate NVIDIA Foundation4D and other autonomous vehicle perception models as well as autolabeling tools for physical AI.
This dataset is for non-commercial uses only.

Intended Usage:
This dataset is intended to support validation, testing, and replication for autonomous vehicle perception models as well as autolabeling tools. Users can use these ground-truth labels to benchmark and validate their own model outputs on the
PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles dataset
.
Dataset Characterization
Data Collection Method
The clips were collected by real-world vehicle fleets. The ground-truth labels were generated from temporally aggregated LiDAR measurements, and machine-generated labels, including 2D semantic labels, 2D instance masks, and 3D cuboid labels.
Labeling Method
Automated
Dataset Format
Format: NCore aux data stored as Zarr v2 in indexed TAR (

Per-voxel occupancy, semantic labels, and velocity

These labels are intended to provide target values and labels that can be used to validate NVIDIA Foundation4D and other autonomous vehicle perception models as well as autolabeling tools for physical AI.
This dataset is for non-commercial uses only.

This dataset is intended to support validation, testing, and replication for autonomous vehicle perception models as well as autolabeling tools. Users can use these ground-truth labels to benchmark and validate their own model outputs on the

The clips were collected by real-world vehicle fleets. The ground-truth labels were generated from temporally aggregated LiDAR measurements, and machine-generated labels, including 2D semantic labels, 2D instance masks, and 3D cuboid labels.

VDEBench: Visual Document Editing Benchmark
Edit the requested text or table. Preserve the rest of the document.
VDEBench evaluates instruction-guided image editing on dense
Chinese and English document pages
. Models must make precise local changes while preserving surrounding text, table structure, typography, and page layout. The benchmark contains
3,506 examples
, covering text replacement, addition, deletion, and table content and structure editing.

Evaluation code
The
VDE-Bench repository
provides data-generation and evaluation tools. The evaluation protocol combines
local edit-region assessment
with
global full-page assessment
to examine both the requested change and its surrounding document context.
OCR and structure evaluation
:
block matching with IoU, text metrics including CDM and BLEU, and TEDS for tables.
Image-quality evaluation
:
PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and CLIP Score.
Layout analysis
:
document-element extraction and layout statistics.
See the repository's
installation and usage instructions
for environment setup, OCR backends, and evaluation commands.

The Gap We're Closing
Open Yap 1K was designed specifically for full-duplex models, in collaboration with researchers, to capture how people speak together naturally in real environments. Instead of having strangers perform prompted conversations, we built a WhatsApp-like app that people used instead of their regular phone calls to talk to friends and family.
We're releasing a serious alternative to speech corpora such as Fisher, Switchboard, and CANDOR. Not only on objective quality measures - 48 kHz, dual-channel, per-track measured metadata - but more importantly on the human elements of speech: the interruptions, overlaps, laughter, backchannels, and variance in prosody. Those elements are the hardest part of the problem and the least represented in the existing literature. Fisher and Switchboard, still the reference points three decades on, recruited strangers, assigned them partners, and in many cases assigned them topics. That was a deliberate design to maximise variety across a fixed budget, and it worked for its era. But both ran over the phone network, which caps usable bandwidth near 4 kHz.
The difference is immediate. Below is a Fisher English clip alongside an Open Yap 1K clip:
Fisher English - 8 kHz, telephone band
Open Yap 1K - 48 kHz, wideband
Newer corpora record at full bandwidth but retain the stranger pairing, and that constraint propagates into the behaviour. Two people who met sixty seconds ago are polite with each other. They take clean turns, they wait for the other to finish, they rarely cut in. It is a conversation, but it is the most cautious version of one - and a full-duplex model trained on it learns a turn-taking policy that real users will violate within the first minute. People who already know each other behave differently. They interrupt, they finish each other's sentences, they backchannel continuously, they laugh over each other, and they leave much shorter gaps between turns. That behaviour is exactly what a full-duplex system has to model, and it is what self-pairing produces for free.
Collection Method
We collect the audio with our own app, which works like a phone call. A speaker invites someone they know, the two of them talk, and both sides are captured as separate tracks. This gives us natural conversation and a straightforward way to scale collection: the incentive to record is that the call was going to happen anyway.
We deliberately collect conversations captured in real environments because it teaches a model robustness - a system that has only heard treated rooms fails in a kitchen. What we do remove is the long tail of genuinely unusable recordings, using several ML models combined into a single screening pipeline.

Intended Use
Speech-to-speech and full-duplex.
Both sides arrive as independent signals on a shared timeline. Interruptions, overlaps and backchannels are preserved rather than collapsed into a single stream, so a model can learn when to start speaking and not only what to say. This is the use case the corpus was designed around, and it is the one where mixed-channel data is least recoverable - once two speakers are summed, the information about who started when is gone.
Expressive TTS.
Spontaneous prosody on clean, isolated 48 kHz tracks. Laughter, fillers, hesitation, and trailing off all appear naturally, because nobody was reading. Word-level timings tag filler, laugh, cough and noise events separately from words, so these can be targeted or excluded during training.
Audio understanding.
Long-form unprompted speech with word-level transcripts for both speakers and per-speaker metadata covering device, headphone state, echo cancellation, measured loudness, and DNSMOS scores over time.
Quality Assurance
Two checks run before a conversation becomes eligible for delivery. A human reviewer rates each conversation for language proficiency, accent classification, naturalness and expressivity. Every transcript then passes an LLM screen for personally identifying information and for content-policy violations; flagged conversations are excluded entirely.
Audio ships un-normalised. Integrated loudness and true peak are measured and reported per track, so a target level can be applied without probing every file.
Transcripts are machine-generated (Deepgram Nova-3, word-level) and are not human-verified.
Consent And Privacy
All audio was recorded on our own platform. Nothing is scraped, mined, or repurposed from elsewhere. Speakers register, give explicit consent before their first recording, and are paid for their time. Demographics are self-reported at registration, before any recording, and are never inferred from audio. Speaker identifiers are pseudonymous and stable within the release. Names, contact details and account identifiers are excluded.
Working With The Sample
The Hub repository holds a hand-picked sample - 8.92 hours, 16 conversations, 8 speakers, CC-BY-4.0 - so you can listen and inspect the schema before deciding whether to request the full corpus.
from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset(
"webdataset",
data_files={"train": "hf://datasets/TheAgenticDataCompany/open-yap-1k/shard-*.tar"},
split="train",
)
sample = ds[0]
a, b = sample["a.flac"]["array"], sample["b.flac"]["array"]
assert len(a) == len(b)   # one timeline, by construction
record = sample["json"]   # metadata and both transcripts
Or fetch the shards and read them with any tar reader:
hf download TheAgenticDataCompany/open-yap-1k \
--repo-type dataset --include "shard-*.tar" --local-dir open-yap-1k
The sample is hand-picked, so its distribution does not represent the full corpus. Each track reports its effective bandwidth in
effective_bandwidth_hz
.

Request - tell us who you are, what you are building, and how the audio will be used.
Review - we read every request and reply within a few hours, either way.
Delivery - approved recipients get a portal account and either a direct download or delivery into their own S3 bucket.
Permitted under the agreement: commercial use including in products you sell; published or internal research; training, fine-tuning and evaluating models, and deploying what you train; internal copies and access for staff and contractors under the same terms.
Not permitted: redistributing, resharing, sublicensing or reselling the dataset; attempting to identify a speaker or link a recording to any external record; creating voice clones or generative reproductions identifiable as a speaker in the corpus.

Nothing is scraped, mined, or repurposed from elsewhere. Speakers register, give explicit consent before their first recording, and are paid for their time. Demographics are self-reported at registration, before any recording, and are never inferred from audio. Speaker identifiers are pseudonymous and stable within the release. Names, contact details and account identifiers are excluded.¦Working With The Sample¦The Hub repository holds a hand-picked sample - 8.92 hours, 16 conversations, 8 speakers, CC-BY-4.0 - so you can listen and inspect the schema before deciding whether to request the full corpus.¦from datasets import load_dataset¦ds = load_dataset(¦"webdataset",¦data_files={"train": "hf://datasets/TheAgenticDataCompany/open-yap-1k/shard-*.tar"},¦split="train",¦)¦sample = ds[0]¦a, b = sample["a.flac"]["array"], sample["b.flac"]["array"]¦assert len(a) == len(b)   # one timeline, by construction¦record = sample["json"]   # metadata and both transcripts¦Or fetch the shards and read them with any tar reader:¦hf download TheAgenticDataCompany/open-yap-1k \¦--repo-type dataset --include "shard-*.tar" --local-dir open-yap-1k¦The sample is hand-picked, so its distribution does not represent the full corpus. Quality controls
Guaranteed by the build and re-checked by
scripts/verify_layers.py
:
2,000-token floor
on every row (user + assistant).
Unique rows
: unique ids, unique assistant texts, unique questions.
No split leakage
: the split is cut on
group_key
(the source entity).
Grounded
: every fact comes from MITRE ATT&CK, D3FEND, CWE, CAPEC, ATLAS,
SigmaHQ, CISA KEV, an RFC, a NIST publication or the cited arXiv paper.
Decontaminated
: no 25-gram overlap with the benchmark corpora, re-checked
by an independent pass.
Defensive only
: no functional exploits, no malware, no weaponised
jailbreak prompts.
Provenance
: every corpus document has a row in
research/fetch_manifest.csv
(url, date, licence).

Reference-appendix share.
Framework entities are short (a KEV entry is a

Task mix.

expert

Dataset Card for ImageNet
Dataset Summary
ILSVRC 2012, commonly known as 'ImageNet' is an image dataset organized according to the WordNet hierarchy. Each meaningful concept in WordNet, possibly described by multiple words or word phrases, is called a "synonym set" or "synset". There are more than 100,000 synsets in WordNet, majority of them are nouns (80,000+). ImageNet aims to provide on average 1000 images to illustrate each synset. Images of each concept are quality-controlled and human-annotated.
💡 This dataset provides access to ImageNet (ILSVRC) 2012 which is the most commonly used
subset
of ImageNet. This dataset spans 1000 object classes and contains 1,281,167 training images, 50,000 validation images and 100,000 test images. The version also has the
patch
which fixes some of the corrupted test set images already applied. For full ImageNet dataset presented in
[2]
, please check the download section of the
main website
.
Supported Tasks and Leaderboards
image-classification
: The goal of this task is to classify a given image into one of 1000 ImageNet classes. The leaderboard is available
here
.
To evaluate the
imagenet-classification
accuracy on the test split, one must first create an account at
https://image-net.org
. This account must be approved by the site administrator. After the account is created, one can submit the results to the test server at
https://image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/eval_server.php
The submission consists of several ASCII text files corresponding to multiple tasks. The task of interest is "Classification submission (top-5 cls error)". A sample of an exported text file looks like the following:
670 778 794 387 650
217 691 564 909 364
737 369 430 531 124
755 930 755 512 152
The export format is described in full in "readme.txt" within the 2013 development kit available here:
https://image-net.org/data/ILSVRC/2013/ILSVRC2013_devkit.tgz
. Please see the section entitled "3.3 CLS-LOC submission format". Briefly, the format of the text file is 100,000 lines corresponding to each image in the test split. Each line of integers correspond to the rank-ordered, top 5 predictions for each test image. The integers are 1-indexed corresponding to the line number in the corresponding labels file. See
imagenet2012_labels.txt
.
Languages
The class labels in the dataset are in English.
Dataset Structure
Data Instances
An example looks like below:
{
'image': <PIL.JpegImagePlugin.JpegImageFile image mode=RGB size=384x512 at 0x276021C5EB8>,
'label': 23
}
Data Fields
The data instances have the following fields:
image
: A
PIL.Image.Image
object containing the image. Note that when accessing the image column:
dataset[0]["image"]
the image file is automatically decoded. Decoding of a large number of image files might take a significant amount of time. Thus it is important to first query the sample index before the
"image"
column,
i.e.
dataset[0]["image"]
should
always
be preferred over
dataset["image"][0]
.
label
: an
int
classification label. -1 for
test
set as the labels are missing.
The labels are indexed based on a sorted list of synset ids such as
n07565083
which we automatically map to original class names. The original dataset is divided into folders based on these synset ids. To get a mapping from original synset names, use the file
LOC_synset_mapping.txt
available on Kaggle challenge page. You can also use
dataset_instance.features["labels"].int2str
function to get the class for a particular label index. Also note that, labels for test set are returned as -1 as they are missing.

Dataset Creation
Curation Rationale
The ImageNet project was inspired by two important needs in computer vision research. The first was the need to establish a clear North Star problem in computer vision. While the field enjoyed an abundance of important tasks to work on, from stereo vision to image retrieval, from 3D reconstruction to image segmentation, object categorization was recognized to be one of the most fundamental capabilities of both human and machine vision. Hence there was a growing demand for a high quality object categorization benchmark with clearly established evaluation metrics. Second, there was a critical need for more data to enable more generalizable machine learning methods. Ever since the birth of the digital era and the availability of web-scale data exchanges, researchers in these fields have been working hard to design more and more sophisticated algorithms to index, retrieve, organize and annotate multimedia data. But good research requires good resources. To tackle this problem at scale (think of your growing personal collection of digital images, or videos, or a commercial web search engine’s database), it was critical to provide researchers with a large-scale image database for both training and testing. The convergence of these two intellectual reasons motivated us to build ImageNet.
Source Data
Initial Data Collection and Normalization
Initial data for ImageNet image classification task consists of photographs collected from
Flickr
and other search engines, manually labeled with the presence of one of 1000 object categories. Constructing ImageNet was an effort to scale up an image classification dataset to cover most nouns in English using tens of millions of manually verified photographs
1
. The image classification task of ILSVRC came as a direct extension of this effort. A subset of categories and images was chosen and fixed to provide a standardized benchmark while the rest of ImageNet continued to grow.
Who are the source language producers?
WordNet synsets further quality controlled by human annotators. The images are from Flickr.
Annotations
Annotation process
The annotation process of collecting ImageNet for image classification task is a three step process.
Defining the 1000 object categories for the image classification task. These categories have evolved over the years.
Collecting the candidate image for these object categories using a search engine.
Quality control on the candidate images by using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to make sure the image has the synset it was collected for.
See the section 3.1 in
1
for more details on data collection procedure and
2
for general information on ImageNet.
Who are the annotators?
Images are automatically fetched from an image search engine based on the synsets and filtered using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk. See
1
for more details.
Personal and Sensitive Information
The 1,000 categories selected for this subset contain only 3 people categories (scuba diver, bridegroom, and baseball player) while the full ImageNet contains 2,832 people categories under the person subtree (accounting for roughly 8.3% of the total images). This subset does contain the images of people without their consent. Though, the study in
[1]
on obfuscating faces of the people in the ImageNet 2012 subset shows that blurring people's faces causes a very minor decrease in accuracy (~0.6%) suggesting that privacy-aware models can be trained on ImageNet. On larger ImageNet, there has been
an attempt
at filtering and balancing the people subtree in the larger ImageNet.
Considerations for Using the Data
Social Impact of Dataset
The ImageNet dataset has been very crucial in advancement of deep learning technology as being the standard benchmark for the computer vision models. The dataset aims to probe models on their understanding of the objects and has become the de-facto dataset for this purpose. ImageNet is still one of the major datasets on which models are evaluated for their generalization in computer vision capabilities as the field moves towards self-supervised algorithms. Please see the future section in
1
for a discussion on social impact of the dataset.
Discussion of Biases
A
study
of the history of the multiple layers (taxonomy, object classes and labeling) of ImageNet and WordNet in 2019 described how bias is deeply embedded in most classification approaches for of all sorts of images.
A
study
has also shown that ImageNet trained models are biased towards texture rather than shapes which in contrast with how humans do object classification. Increasing the shape bias improves the accuracy and robustness.

ILSVRC 2012, commonly known as 'ImageNet' is an image dataset organized according to the WordNet hierarchy. Each meaningful concept in WordNet, possibly described by multiple words or word phrases, is called a "synonym set" or "synset". There are more than 100,000 synsets in WordNet, majority of them are nouns (80,000+). ImageNet aims to provide on average 1000 images to illustrate each synset. Images of each concept are quality-controlled and human-annotated.

The ImageNet project was inspired by two important needs in computer vision research. The first was the need to establish a clear North Star problem in computer vision. While the field enjoyed an abundance of important tasks to work on, from stereo vision to image retrieval, from 3D reconstruction to image segmentation, object categorization was recognized to be one of the most fundamental capabilities of both human and machine vision. Hence there was a growing demand for a high quality object categorization benchmark with clearly established evaluation metrics. Second, there was a critical need for more data to enable more generalizable machine learning methods. Ever since the birth of the digital era and the availability of web-scale data exchanges, researchers in these fields have been working hard to design more and more sophisticated algorithms to index, retrieve, organize and annotate multimedia data. But good research requires good resources. To tackle this problem at scale (think of your growing personal collection of digital images, or videos, or a commercial web search engine’s database), it was critical to provide researchers with a large-scale image database for both training and testing. The convergence of these two intellectual reasons motivated us to build ImageNet.
Initial data for ImageNet image classification task consists of photographs collected from

and other search engines, manually labeled with the presence of one of 1000 object categories. Constructing ImageNet was an effort to scale up an image classification dataset to cover most nouns in English using tens of millions of manually verified photographs

. The image classification task of ILSVRC came as a direct extension of this effort. A subset of categories and images was chosen and fixed to provide a standardized benchmark while the rest of ImageNet continued to grow.
Who are the source language producers?
WordNet synsets further quality controlled by human annotators. The images are from Flickr.
The annotation process of collecting ImageNet for image classification task is a three step process.
Defining the 1000 object categories for the image classification task. These categories have evolved over the years.
Collecting the candidate image for these object categories using a search engine.
Quality control on the candidate images by using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to make sure the image has the synset it was collected for.

The 1,000 categories selected for this subset contain only 3 people categories (scuba diver, bridegroom, and baseball player) while the full ImageNet contains 2,832 people categories under the person subtree (accounting for roughly 8.3% of the total images). This subset does contain the images of people without their consent. Though, the study in

on obfuscating faces of the people in the ImageNet 2012 subset shows that blurring people's faces causes a very minor decrease in accuracy (~0.6%) suggesting that privacy-aware models can be trained on ImageNet. On larger ImageNet, there has been
at filtering and balancing the people subtree in the larger ImageNet.

The ImageNet dataset has been very crucial in advancement of deep learning technology as being the standard benchmark for the computer vision models. The dataset aims to probe models on their understanding of the objects and has become the de-facto dataset for this purpose. ImageNet is still one of the major datasets on which models are evaluated for their generalization in computer vision capabilities as the field moves towards self-supervised algorithms. for a discussion on social impact of the dataset.

Rationale¦The ImageNet project was inspired by two important needs in computer vision research. The first was the need to establish a clear North Star problem in computer vision. While the field enjoyed an abundance of important tasks to work on, from stereo vision to image retrieval, from 3D reconstruction to image segmentation, object categorization was recognized to be one of the most fundamental capabilities of both human and machine vision. Hence there was a growing demand for a high quality object categorization benchmark with clearly established evaluation metrics. Second, there was a critical need for more data to enable more generalizable machine learning methods. Ever since the birth of the digital era and the availability of web-scale data exchanges, researchers in these fields have been working hard to design more and more sophisticated algorithms to index, retrieve, organize and annotate multimedia data. But good research requires good resources. To tackle this problem at scale (think of your growing personal collection of digital images, or videos, or a commercial web search engine’s database), it was critical to provide researchers with a large-scale image database for both training and testing. The convergence of these two intellectual reasons motivated us to build ImageNet.¦Source Data¦Initial Data Collection and Normalization¦Initial data for ImageNet image classification task consists of photographs collected from¦Flickr¦and other search engines, manually labeled with the presence of one of 1000 object categories. Constructing ImageNet was an effort to scale up an image classification dataset to cover most nouns in English using tens of millions of manually verified photographs¦1¦. The image classification task of ILSVRC came as a direct extension of this effort. A subset of categories and images was chosen and fixed to provide a standardized benchmark while the rest of ImageNet continued to grow.¦Who are the source language producers?¦WordNet synsets further quality controlled by human annotators. The images are from Flickr.¦Annotations¦Annotation process¦The annotation process of collecting ImageNet for image classification task is a three step process.¦Defining the 1000 object categories for the image classification task. These categories have evolved over the years.¦Collecting the candidate image for these object categories using a search engine.¦Quality control on the candidate images by using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to make sure the image has the synset it was collected for.¦See the section 3.1 in¦1¦for more details on data collection procedure and¦2¦for general information on ImageNet.¦Who are the annotators?¦Images are automatically fetched from an image search engine based on the synsets and filtered using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk. See¦1¦for more details.¦Personal and Sensitive Information¦The 1,000 categories selected for this subset contain only 3 people categories (scuba diver, bridegroom, and baseball player) while the full ImageNet contains 2,832 people categories under the person subtree (accounting for roughly 8.3% of the total images). This subset does contain the images of people without their consent. Though, the study in¦[1]¦on obfuscating faces of the people in the ImageNet 2012 subset shows that blurring people's faces causes a very minor decrease in accuracy (~0.6%) suggesting that privacy-aware models can be trained on ImageNet. On larger ImageNet, there has been¦an attempt¦at filtering and balancing the people subtree in the larger ImageNet.¦Considerations for Using the Data¦Social Impact of Dataset¦The ImageNet dataset has been very crucial in advancement of deep learning technology as being the standard benchmark for the computer vision models. The dataset aims to probe models on their understanding of the objects and has become the de-facto dataset for this purpose. ImageNet is still one of the major datasets on which models are evaluated for their generalization in computer vision capabilities as the field moves towards self-supervised algorithms. Increasing the shape bias improves the accuracy and robustness.¦Another¦study¦more potential issues and biases with the ImageNet dataset and provides an alternative benchmark for image classification task. Scaling Data Environments from Scratch
Specify the world behind the files. Generate the data. Ground the supervision.
DataWorld-Train-2k-part1 — the training slice (part 1 of 2)
2,135 tasks
in exactly the same
harbor
task format
as
Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Bench
,
and graded by the same harness. One self-contained directory per task, each
carrying its own copy of the world's data, nothing mounted from a sibling task.
This repository is part 1: it holds 597 of those 2,135 tasks
— every task whose
world id is
p000499
or below. Part 2 is
Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Train-2k-part2
,
which holds the other 1,538 tasks (world ids
p000500
–
p009920
). The Hub caps a
repository at 1,000,000 files and the slice contains 1,011,712, so it ships as two
repositories split on world id: no world is split across the two, and the union is
exactly the 2,135 tasks, with nothing duplicated and nothing dropped.
Format
dataworld-train-2k-part1/
├── README.md
├── sample_manifest.json      # task list + provenance (describes the full slice)
├── synthesis_data_input.json # {input, target} pairs, paths rewritten relative
├── manifest.jsonl            # per-task metadata (world / layer / kind / dag category)
├── dataworld-pXXXXXX-<cause|consequence>-<N>/   # × 589 task directories
└── _archived-tasks/          # × 8 tasks, one .tar.gz each (see below)
Each task directory is an ordinary
harbor
task —
instruction.md
,
task.toml
,
environment/
(Dockerfile + a self-contained copy of the world's
data) and
tests/
(verifier, judge client,
rubric.json
) — so any one of them
can be built, run and verified on its own. The three metadata files describe the
full
2,135-task slice in both repositories; entries for tasks that live in the
other repository resolve there. As in the benchmark, the two files that would give
the answer away (
WORLD.md
,
dag.json
) are absent, and the image build asserts
their absence.
Two layout adaptations (part 1 only)
All 2,135 tasks are present and
no instruction, rubric or data file was
edited
, but two things could not be shipped verbatim here because the Hub caps a
folder at 10,000 entries:
14 data folders are sharded into
shard-00/
,
shard-01/
, … subfolders
(the files keep their names and bytes, only one level
of path was added, and nothing in those tasks refers to the folders by name), and
8 tasks ship as
_archived-tasks/<task>.tar.gz
instead of directories, because
there the oversized folder
is
referenced by path from inside the data
(
p000165-consequence-1..4
,
p000026-cause-1/2/4
,
p000026-consequence-3
) —
tar xzf
one and you get the original task directory back, byte-identical.
Both adaptations concern worlds below the
p000500
boundary, so
part 2 ships
every task as a plain directory
— no shards and no
_archived-tasks/
there.
Scoring
Same harness and same scale as
DataWorld-Bench
:
reward = 100 * (raw - lo) / (hi - lo)
in
[0, 100]
, with
timeout_sec = 28800.0
,
cpus = 8
,
memory_mb = 16384
and the same placeholders
in
tests/judge.env
. Task content is
not
shared — the two datasets have zero
tasks in common, since bench and training worlds do not intersect.
Running a task
Build
environment/Dockerfile
, run the agent as user
agent
(its report must
land at
/app/answer.txt
), then run
tests/test.sh
as user
verifier
after
filling in
tests/judge.env
. For the 8 tasks in
_archived-tasks/
, extract the
tarball first so that the task directory sits next to the others.

🛡️ Cybersecurity Deep Dive: Attack & Defense
⚔️ Why This Matters
Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed in security-critical environments—yet most open-source training data ignores real-world adversarial scenarios.
The Open Distillation Codex
includes a dedicated
cybersecurity
category designed to equip models with:
Attack Awareness
: Recognize and generate realistic attack patterns, exploits, penetration testing commands, and social engineering dialogues.
Defense Proficiency
: Learn to propose defensive measures, detect anomalies, and articulate incident response protocols.
Exploit Understanding
: Analyze and explain software vulnerabilities, craft proof-of-concept code (for educational purposes), and understand exploit chains.
Red/Blue Team Simulation
: Engage in multi-turn conversations mimicking red team attack planning and blue team defense coordination.
Threat Intelligence
: Summarize, classify, and reason about cyber threat reports, CVEs, and IOCs (Indicators of Compromise).
This makes the dataset a powerful foundation for building
cybersecurity-aware LLMs
,
security co-pilots
, and
automated vulnerability assessment tools
.

"Explain how an attacker could exploit a vulnerable login form using SQL injection. Provide a sample malicious input."

"An attacker could bypass authentication by injecting SQL logic. For a query like:
`SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='$user' AND password='$pass'`,
the attacker might enter `admin' --` as the username and anything as password. The resulting query becomes:
`SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' --' AND password='...'`
The `--` comments out the password check, granting access as admin. More advanced attacks use UNION to extract data."
"As a red team operator, list the steps you would take after gaining initial access to a Windows machine using a phishing payload."

"1. Establish persistence: `schtasks /create /tn "Updater" /tr "C:\malware.exe" /sc hourly`
2. Enumerate local users: `net user /domain`
3. Dump credentials: `mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords`
4. Lateral movement: use PsExec to move to file server.
5. Exfiltrate data: compress sensitive files and upload via DNS tunneling.
Always maintain C2 communication over HTTPS to blend in."
"An IDS alert flags unusual outbound DNS traffic from a workstation. What's the immediate response?"

"1. Isolate the workstation from the network (VLAN change or port shutdown).
2. Capture volatile memory and network logs for forensics.
3. Check DNS queries: if long, random-looking subdomains, suspect DNS tunneling.
4. Scan for malware with updated signatures.
5. Review firewall logs for similar traffic from other hosts.
6. If confirmed, initiate incident response playbook for data exfiltration."

Scaling Data Environments from Scratch
Specify the world behind the files. Generate the data. Ground the supervision.
DataWorld-Bench
A 100-task benchmark for agentic, evidence-grounded data analysis.
Each task
drops an agent into a self-contained business world, hands it a multi-system pile
of raw data, and asks for a conclusion that a strict LLM judge then grades against
a task-specific rubric.
Format
Every task is one directory, and a directory of task directories
is
the dataset —
nothing else has to be configured to point a harness at this repository.
DataWorld-Bench/
├── README.md
├── sample_manifest.json                          # metadata for the 100 tasks
└── dataworld-pXXXXXX-<cause|consequence>-<1|2>/  # × 100 task directories
Each task directory is an ordinary
harbor
task
:
instruction.md
,
task.toml
,
environment/
(Dockerfile + a
self-contained copy of the world's data) and
tests/
(verifier, judge client,
rubric.json
). Tasks share no state and mount nothing from a sibling task, so any
one of them can be built, run and verified on its own.
pXXXXXX
is the id of the source world,
cause
/
consequence
is the task
kind (every world contributes exactly one of each), and the trailing
1
/
2
is the variant index within that kind.
Per task: 4–12 subsystems (mean ≈ 7), 1.2 MB – 6.1 GB (median ≈ 85 MB) and
8 – 10.6k files (median ≈ 31); the whole repository is ≈ 50.2k files / 50.7 GB.
The two files that would give the answer away (
WORLD.md
,
dag.json
) are absent
from the corpus and asserted absent inside the image.
task.toml
is harbor
schema_version = "1.1"
, one envelope for all 100 tasks:
[agent] timeout_sec = 28800.0
(8 h),
[verifier] timeout_sec = 1200.0
,
[environment] cpus = 8
,
memory_mb = 16384
,
storage_mb = 10240
,
allow_internet = true
.
Scoring
The judge returns one verdict per rubric criterion, and the raw score is
normalized against that task's own reachable bounds:
reward = 100 * (raw - lo) / (hi - lo)        # in [0, 100]
All positive criteria satisfied =
100
, all negative criteria triggered =
0
.
A missing or empty
/app/answer.txt
is a blank submission and scores
0
; a
grading-infrastructure failure
also
writes
0
but carries a
judge_error
key in
details.json
—
detect failures via
judge_error
, never via the value
.
Running a task
Build the image from
environment/Dockerfile
, run the agent as user
agent
(its
report must land at
/app/answer.txt
), then run
tests/test.sh
as user
verifier
.
tests/judge.env
selects the judge through ordinary environment
variables (
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL
/
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN
/
ANTHROPIC_MODEL
, or the
JUDGE_*
equivalents) and ships with placeholders. The Dockerfile builds on the
public
quay.io/jupyter/scipy-notebook
image, pinned to a dated tag, and needs no
configuration.

Tasks share no state and mount nothing from a sibling task, so any¦one of them can be built, run and verified on its own.¦pXXXXXX¦is the id of the source world,¦cause¦/¦consequence¦is the task¦kind (every world contributes exactly one of each), and the trailing¦1¦/¦2¦is the variant index within that kind.¦Per task: 4–12 subsystems (mean ≈ 7), 1.2 MB – 6.1 GB (median ≈ 85 MB) and¦8 – 10.6k files (median ≈ 31); the whole repository is ≈ 50.2k files / 50.7 GB.¦The two files that would give the answer away (¦WORLD.md¦,¦dag.json¦) are absent¦from the corpus and asserted absent inside the image.¦task.toml¦is harbor¦schema_version = "1.1"¦, one envelope for all 100 tasks:¦[agent] timeout_sec = 28800.0¦(8 h),¦[verifier] timeout_sec = 1200.0¦,¦[environment] cpus = 8¦,¦memory_mb = 16384¦,¦storage_mb = 10240¦,¦allow_internet = true¦.¦Scoring¦The judge returns one verdict per rubric criterion, and the raw score is¦normalized against that task's own reachable bounds:¦reward = 100 * (raw - lo) / (hi - lo)        # in [0, 100]¦All positive criteria satisfied =¦100¦, all negative criteria triggered =¦0¦.¦A missing or empty¦/app/answer.txt¦is a blank submission and scores¦0¦; a¦grading-infrastructure failure¦also¦writes¦0¦but carries a¦judge_error¦key in¦details.json¦—¦detect failures via¦judge_error¦, never via the value¦.¦Running a task¦Build the image from¦environment/Dockerfile¦, run the agent as user¦agent¦(its¦report must land at¦/app/answer.txt¦), then run¦tests/test.sh¦as user¦verifier¦.¦tests/judge.env¦selects the judge through ordinary environment¦variables (¦ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL¦/¦ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN¦/¦ANTHROPIC_MODEL¦, or the¦JUDGE_*¦equivalents) and ships with placeholders. The Dockerfile builds on the¦public¦quay.io/jupyter/scipy-notebook¦image, pinned to a dated tag, and needs no¦configuration.¦Links¦Project page —¦https://zhanli-li.github.io/Data-World/¦Paper —¦https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21656¦Code, data generation pipeline and evaluation harness —¦https://github.com/Zhanli-Li/Data-World¦Full collection —¦https://huggingface.co/collections/Zhanli-Li/dataworld¦License¦Released under the¦Apache License 2.0¦— see¦LICENSE¦.¦Copy to bucket¦Downloads last month¦3,179¦Total file size:¦50.7 GB¦Collection including¦Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Bench¦DataWorld¦Collection¦Agentic RL fine-tune of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B for data analysis & cowork , plus its 100-task held-out evaluation benchmark.¦•¦5 items¦•¦Updated¦6 days ago¦•¦8¦Paper for¦Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Bench¦Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch¦Paper¦•¦2610.21656¦•¦Published¦17 days ago¦•¦40¦System theme¦Company¦TOS¦Privacy¦About¦Careers¦Website¦Models¦Datasets¦Spaces¦Pricing¦Docs

DataWorld-Train-2k-part2 — the training slice (part 2 of 2)
2,135 tasks
in exactly the same
harbor
task format
as
Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Bench
,
and graded by the same harness. One self-contained directory per task, each
carrying its own copy of the world's data, nothing mounted from a sibling task.
This repository is part 2: it holds 1,538 of those 2,135 tasks
— every task
whose world id is
p000500
or above. Part 1 is
Zhanli-Li/DataWorld-Train-2k-part1
,
which holds the other 597 tasks (world ids
p000000
–
p000499
). The Hub caps a
repository at 1,000,000 files and the slice contains 1,011,712, so it ships as two
repositories split on world id: no world is split across the two, and the union is
exactly the 2,135 tasks, with nothing duplicated and nothing dropped.
Format
dataworld-train-2k-part2/
├── README.md
├── sample_manifest.json      # task list + provenance (describes the full slice)
├── synthesis_data_input.json # {input, target} pairs, paths rewritten relative
├── manifest.jsonl            # per-task metadata (world / layer / kind / dag category)
└── dataworld-pXXXXXX-<cause|consequence>-<N>/   # × 1,538 task directories
Each task directory is an ordinary
harbor
task —
instruction.md
,
task.toml
,
environment/
(Dockerfile + a self-contained copy of the world's
data) and
tests/
(verifier, judge client,
rubric.json
) — so any one of them
can be built, run and verified on its own. The three metadata files describe the
full
2,135-task slice in both repositories; entries for tasks that live in the
other repository resolve there. As in the benchmark, the two files that would give

WORLD.md
,
dag.json

—
concern only worlds below the
p000500
boundary and therefore live in part 1:
there is no
_archived-tasks/
here and no sharded folder.

MarathonDocBench
A New Benchmark for Ultra-Long Document Parsing: Targeting Hundred-Page-Scale Documents.
MarathonDocBench is the first benchmark specifically designed for
hundred-page document parsing
. It contains 100 documents spanning
100–300 pages
(~18k pages, ~205k annotated layout elements, mixed Chinese/English), with rich cross-page structures — cross-page text and tables appear frequently and densely across documents. Structural annotations (bounding boxes, block type, hierarchy, reading order, and cross-page continuations of text and tables) are initialized from a strong page-by-page parser and carefully refined by human annotators; content transcriptions are verified through an iterative VLM-based refinement pipeline, with flagged disagreements adjudicated by human annotators.
This repository ships the
data
(page images + ground-truth annotations).
Evaluation reuses the
MPDocBench-Parse
toolkit — see
Usage
below.
1. Dataset
MarathonDocBench.json        # ground-truth annotations (100 documents)
images/
├── PDF1/page_1.png …
├── PDF1/page_2.png …
├── PDF1/ …                  # one folder of page images per document
├── PDF2/page_1.png
└── …                        # ~18k PNG pages total
Each entry in
MarathonDocBench.json
follows the MPDocBench schema (
page_info
/
layout_dets
/
extra
):
layout_dets
carries per-element
category_type
,
text
/
html
/
latex
, reading
order
, heading
anno_id
, and
poly
boxes;
extra.relation
lists cross-page
truncated
merges.
2. Usage
Evaluate with the
MPDocBench-Parse
toolkit; this dataset is a drop-in ground-truth replacement (same schema, same eight metrics).
# 1. Get the toolkit
git
clone
https://github.com/Tongyi-Zhiwen/Qwen-Doc.git
cd
Qwen-Doc/MPDocBench
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install mmeval
# needed by the dataset loader, not pinned upstream
# 1b. Replace 3 evaluator files with the accelerated drop-in from THIS repo
#     (metric-identical; only adds doc-level parallelism + a configurable match
#     timeout — vanilla hardcodes a 30s serial match that under-scores ultra-long
#     docs and can take days). Overwrites dataset/end2end_dataset.py,
#     metrics/cal_metric.py and utils/data_preprocess.py:
cp
-r /path/to/MarathonDocBench/utils/mpdocbench_patch/* .
# 2. Place this dataset where the config can find it, e.g.
#    data/MarathonDocBench.json   and   data/images/...
# 3. Generate predictions: one Markdown file per document, named <doc_id>.md
#    (e.g. mp3lan_0101.md). Figure tags must follow the required format:
#        ![](pageN_x1_y1_x2_y2.jpg)
#    (N = 1-based page index; x1,y1,x2,y2 = integer coords on a 1000x1000 grid.)
#    Any parser is fine, as long as figure tags follow this format.
# 4. Point configs/end2end.yaml at the dataset (ground_truth.data_path ->
#    data/MarathonDocBench.json, prediction.data_path -> predictions/your_model_md),
#    then run with the settings used for the leaderboard. MPDOC_TEDS_TIMEOUT is
#    required: a few tables have tens of thousands of cells and pure-Python TEDS
#    would run for hours on them; past the cap such a table scores 0.
MPDOC_EVAL_NPROC=32 MPDOC_MATCH_TIMEOUT=1800 MPDOC_DOC_BUDGET=0 \
MPDOC_TEDS_NPROC=32 MPDOC_TEDS_TIMEOUT=300 \
python pdf_validation.py --config ./configs/end2end.yaml
Per-metric results are written to
result/
. The leaderboard
Overall
is the mean of the eight metrics — compute it from the per-metric outputs.
Running a general VLM.
Whole-document inference can fail on provider caps: too many input images per request, request/JSON size limits, or the output-token ceiling (long docs truncate mid-table). Our competitor baselines send all pages in one request, progressively downscale images on oversize/timeout and retry, skip docs over the image cap, and leave failures as empty predictions so the denominator stays 100.
Evaluation notes.
Headings must be real Markdown headings (
#
,
##
, …) — emphasis such as
**bold**
is NOT counted as a heading (it will lower HeadingTEDS). Figure page attribution is part of the score: a figure tagged with the wrong
pageN
is matched against the wrong page and penalized by FigureF1. The documents are very long; with the accelerated evaluator above (
MPDOC_EVAL_NPROC
+ a large
MPDOC_MATCH_TIMEOUT
) a full 100-document run takes tens of minutes instead of hours.

FineART: Fine-Grained Annotated Robotic Trajectory Dataset
FineART is co-released by
Scale AI
and
Hugging Face LeRobot
. The data was collected and annotated by the Physical AI unit at
Scale AI
.
FineART is a bimanual manipulation dataset where
every episode comes with dense, human-written subtask annotations
. It has
40,543 teleoperated episodes (1,718 hours)
,
533,913 subtask labels
, and
151 tasks
, all collected on a Trossen Stationary AI (ALOHA-style) bimanual robot.
Most robot datasets give one instruction per episode, or label subtasks for only part of their hours. In FineART the whole dataset is annotated: episodes average about 2.5 minutes and about 13 subtasks, so models can be trained directly on step-by-step language.
Dense subtask language makes FineART suited to training
hierarchical (System 1 / System 2) policies
: a high-level policy (System 2) that reads the task and predicts the next subtask in language, and a low-level policy (System 1) that conditions on that subtask to produce actions. In this spirit we also launched
FineART-VLA
, a single policy that predicts its own next subtask and then acts on it (see
FineART-VLA
below).

Annotations
Whole-episode text summary with execution-quality / success metadata; contiguous, non-overlapping subtask segments with free-text descriptions
Annotations were written by human annotators (no VLM assistance), separate from the teleoperators, and audited by a third team. They are specific: colors are mentioned in 81% of object mentions, and same-class objects are disambiguated 81% of the time (e.g. "the red cup" vs "the blue cup").

Train directly on step-by-step language
LeRobot's recipe layer turns the rows above into chat-style samples on the fly, with no preprocessing. A minimal recipe that asks the model to predict the active subtask from the episode task:
messages:
-
{
role:
user
,
content:
"${task}"
,
stream:
high_level
}
-
{
role:
assistant
,
content:
"${subtask}"
,
stream:
low_level
,
target:
true
}
${subtask}
is bound to
active_at(t, style=subtask)
at each frame. See the LeRobot docs page
Language columns and recipes
and the
subtask_mem
recipes for blends (high-level subtask prediction + low-level execution). FineART-VLA is trained this way.

Tips
Imbalanced tasks.
About 77% of hours are everyday pick-and-place/sorting. If you want the contact-rich long tail represented, sample by task (use
task_index
) rather than uniformly over frames.
Large dataset.
~185M frames of 4-camera video. Use
episodes=[...]
or
StreamingLeRobotDataset
for experiments; use a
DataLoader
with several workers and
video_backend="pyav"
/
"torchcodec"
for training.
Timestamps are episode-relative seconds
, the same clock as the frame
timestamp
, so subtask alignment needs no conversion.
FineART-VLA
FineART-VLA
is our single policy that predicts its own next subtask in language and then acts on it. Mid-training on FineART's subtask annotations raised success on a spatial-instruction task from 32% to 100% and on a long-horizon task (with human subtask guidance) from 16% to 76%. On a new robot (YAM), FineART mid-training matched baseline performance with about 10× less fine-tuning data. See the paper for details.

Code:
github.com/Cohere-Labs-Community/CulturalRiddles
A community-built benchmark of original cultural riddles from
62 communities across 51 languages and 45 countries
, written by 167 native speakers. Each riddle describes something without naming it, so answering it takes cultural knowledge, not translation or web search. A native speaker recognises the answer at once; a model succeeds only if it carries that culture's knowledge.
The release has four tables:
Table
Rows
What it holds
riddles
(default)
6,191
The riddles and their reference answers.
model_answers
170,520
Every answer from 28 model configurations on the 6,090 benchmarked riddles, with its final score and who scored it.
human_annotations
74,383
Every native-speaker label on a unique answer, including independent second labels.
models
28
The model configurations, their sizes, and their recorded reasoning settings.
Why riddles
A riddle names nothing. "This red-crossed sphere's juice is not sweet for your stomach" means nothing to a search engine, but every Hungarian recognises Unicum, a famous bitters. A model that only knows the formal name misses it. Because each riddle is original, unpublished, and culturally specific, it resists memorisation and lookup.
Languages and communities
The unit is the present-day national-linguistic community, for example Spanish in Argentina or Bengali in India. Languages and communities differ because several communities share a language: Argentine, Cuban, and Peruvian riddles are all in Spanish but draw on three cultures. 1,234 riddles come from topics each community chose itself. the list of communities
.

Curation
Every riddle is original human writing by native speakers writing for their own community. AI tools may be used for brainstorming or to test difficulty, but the riddles are written by people. English translations are for human reference only, never shown to a model. The data contains no names or contact details of writers or annotators.
Intended use and terms
The data is released under the terms in
LICENSE
: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 attribution terms combined with an evaluation-only restriction.
This data must not be used to train, fine-tune, or distill models, nor as seeds for synthetic data generation.
It is an evaluation benchmark; training on it contaminates future measurement. This applies to the model answers and labels as much as to the riddles.
Content note
Although we have filtered the dataset for harmful content, some riddles may still contain sensitive themes or potentially problematic ideas. These are presented solely as cultural and linguistic puzzles, not as endorsements of the views expressed or guidance for real-world behavior.
Riddles flagged in a content review carry a short content note in their
riddle_note
field. Model answers are published as generated and were not filtered: many are hallucinated, and some may be offensive.

A community-built benchmark of original cultural riddles from

, written by 167 native speakers. Each riddle describes something without naming it, so answering it takes cultural knowledge, not translation or web search. A native speaker recognises the answer at once; a model succeeds only if it carries that culture's knowledge.
The riddles and their reference answers.
Every answer from 28 model configurations on the 6,090 benchmarked riddles, with its final score and who scored it.
Every native-speaker label on a unique answer, including independent second labels.
The model configurations, their sizes, and their recorded reasoning settings.

A riddle names nothing. "This red-crossed sphere's juice is not sweet for your stomach" means nothing to a search engine, but every Hungarian recognises Unicum, a famous bitters. A model that only knows the formal name misses it. Because each riddle is original, unpublished, and culturally specific, it resists memorisation and lookup.

The unit is the present-day national-linguistic community, for example Spanish in Argentina or Bengali in India. Languages and communities differ because several communities share a language: Argentine, Cuban, and Peruvian riddles are all in Spanish but draw on three cultures. 1,234 riddles come from topics each community chose itself. 3DCodeVerse-2M
A large-scale corpus of standalone, executable 3D code
— Blender Python, CadQuery, GLSL, Three.js, OpenSCAD and URDF — released with the paper
3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
.

Collection
Each program is packaged with the files it needs to run in its declared environment, plus rendered views,
captions (instruction / detailed description / construction procedure) and, where available, meshes and
verification records. The
default
config merges everything into
2,028,286 training rows
(program × caption type)
on one schema, ready for
datasets
and LLaMA-Factory.
Quick start
from
datasets
import
load_dataset
ds = load_dataset(
"3dcodeverse/3dcodeverse-2m"
, split=
"text"
)
# 2,028,286 rows, text only
ds = ds.
filter
(
lambda
r: r[
"source"
] ==
"deepcad"
and
r[
"caption_type"
] ==
"instruction"
)
Each row is a ShareGPT record (
system
,
conversations
= human prompt → gpt code) plus filter columns:
source
,
subset
,
variant
,
caption_type
,
compiles
,
repair
,
n_tokens
,
model
.
Nothing is pre-filtered — e.g. GLSL rows with
compiles == False
are kept, so select with a predicate.

Layout
<source>/                         one folder per origin
<subset>/<sample>/              a self-contained, runnable sample
code.py | *.html | *.scad …   the program
meta.json                     id, language, environment, source, license, renders[]
captions.json                 {instruction, detailed, …}
renders/                      multi-view PNGs (+ object.glb where available)
<subset>_llamafactory*/         the same samples as ShareGPT parquet
(_text = text prompt, _img / _imgtext = with reference renders)
pair_renders/                   448px JPEG renders referenced by the _img / _imgtext rows
data/text/                        all *_llamafactory* text rows merged on one schema (default config)
viewer/                           one row per sample for the dataset viewer (index config)
_reports/                         QC records: folder index, dedup, GLSL compile reports
dataset_info_text.json            LLaMA-Factory registry, text-only subsets
dataset_info_image.json           LLaMA-Factory registry, image subsets

Known Caveats
Arabic orthography.
The
llm_generated
portion of
jabarti
was written
without hamza forms (~5 per 1k chars against ~28 in native Arabic Wikipedia)
and essentially without diacritics. Those records are flagged
ortho_stripped = true
; filter or down-weight them if standard orthography
matters for your model.
Overlapping coverage.
jabarti
and
cohere-wiki
both draw on Wikipedia,
so some articles appear under both sources with different chunk boundaries.
Exact-duplicate text is removed; re-chunked duplicates are retained
deliberately, acting as upsampling of that content.

GAIA dataset
GAIA is a benchmark which aims at evaluating next-generation LLMs (LLMs with augmented capabilities due to added tooling, efficient prompting, access to search, etc).
We added gating to prevent bots from scraping the dataset. Please do not reshare the validation or test set in a crawlable format.
Data and leaderboard
GAIA is made of more than 450 non-trivial question with an unambiguous answer, requiring different levels of tooling and autonomy to solve. It is therefore divided in 3 levels, where level 1 should be breakable by very good LLMs, and level 3 indicate a strong jump in model capabilities. Each level is divided into a fully public dev set for validation, and a test set with private answers and metadata.
GAIA leaderboard can be found in this space (
https://huggingface.co/spaces/gaia-benchmark/leaderboard
).
Questions are contained in metadata.jsonl. Some questions come with an additional file, that can be found in the same folder and whose id is given in the field file_name.
More details in
the paper
for now and soon here as well.

To keep GAIA compatible with HF datasets 4.x where code-based dataset loaders are deprecated—we now ship Parquet-backed splits that mirror the former JSONL structure:
metadata.parquet
carries the full split, and companion files like
metadata.level1.parquet
retain the per-level views exposed in the configs.

, so existing processing pipelines can continue unchanged.

2023/test/<attachment-id>.pdf
), ensuring offline access to PDFs, media, and other auxiliary files.

Frequently Asked Questions
Find answers to common questions about Spaces
Is there a limit of how many Spaces I can have?
Static Spaces are free for everyone with no limit. Gradio and Docker Spaces run on compute and require a paid plan (PRO for individuals, Team or Enterprise for organizations).
Can I use secrets?
Yes, Spaces have secrets management so you don't have to hardcode tokens or keys into your application.
Can I use a GPU?
You can
upgrade your Space to use a GPU
, or even
✉️ request a free community grant
if you are building a cool demo!
What is the hardware limit?
Each environment is currently limited to 16GB RAM and 8 CPU cores.
Where can I learn more about Streamlit and Gradio?
Gradio
and
Streamlit
are very easy to learn and use. We suggest you to check their respective sites.
Can I add my tool for building apps?
Please
contact us
if you would like to use your own tool to build apps.
Where can I read the documentation?
You can find the official Spaces documentation at
https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces
.
Where can I ask questions if I need help?
For general feedback post to this
discussion
, for specific questions go to the
forum
.
